articles.text: Nate Redinbo On Monday, February 1, Piedmont’s City Council unanimously approved a second reading of the proposed reach codes. Ordinance 750 N.S. amends City Code regarding requirements for energy efficiency measures, photovoltaic systems, and all-electric construction in new or existing low-rise residential buildings. Ordinance 751 N.S. amends City Code to include requirements for the preparation of a Home Energy Audit or Home Energy Score for low-rise residential buildings. City staff initiated the process for adopting the reach codes in 2019. Along the way, there have been two public opinion surveys, several workshops, virtual town halls, two City Council meetings, and lots of feedback from community members. Now that the reach codes have been adopted, what does that mean for residents? The proposed changes can lead to additional requirements during building projects, but not immediately. Ordinance 750 N.S. will be sent to the California Energy Commission (CEC), where it will verify that the codes are at least as stringent as the California Energy Code. The reach codes are then posted for public comment for 60 days. At the end of the public comment period, CEC will approve or return the codes for edits. Additionally, the reach codes must be sent to the California Building Standards Commission for approval. If both of these commissions approve the reach codes, they will become part of the City’s building code. This means that projects will have to start abiding by them upon this approval date. We set an effective date so that the public will have ample notice of a definitive date that Ordinance 750 N.S. will go into effect on June 1, 2021. This is four months from today. Each project that requires a permit will work with a member of the City’s Planning Department, who will be able to explain the reach code requirements to applicants. Ordinance 751 N.S. will go into effect on March 3, which is 30 days after City Council approved the code.

articles.text: Larceny theft, motor vehicle theft, and burglary has increased in Piedmont, according to an end-of-year crime report given by Police Chief Jeremy Bowers at Monday night’s City Council meeting. More arrests related to Automated License Plate Readers (ALPRs) were made last year than in 2019. Piedmont police officers made 17 arrests and recovered 34 stolen vehicles in events directly related to ALPR cameras. But Piedmont experienced more than a 50 percent increase in reportable offenses in 2020 as compared to 2019, from 244 offenses in 2019 to 370 offenses in 2020. The large increase was most notably due to increases in theft, auto theft and residential burglary, which has steadily increased in recent years. For example, the total number of reported larcenies in 2018 was 123, which increased to 162 in 2019, and doubled last year to 236 reported offenses of larceny theft. Motor vehicle theft tripled from 19 reported offenses in 2019, to 60 auto thefts last year. Recovered vehicle values have lowered from 2018 to 2020, however. In 2019, $257,800 worth of valuables were recovered total, in 2020, only $167,300 worth of valuables were recovered. “While the Police Department continuously conducts proactive patrols to mitigate thefts and other crimes, we cannot overemphasize the importance of residents and visitors employing basic crime prevention actions such as not leaving valuables in vehicles,” City Administrator Sara Lillevand stated in a staff report. articles.text: Piedmont School District and its teachers’ union, the Association of Piedmont teachers (APT), reached a tentative agreement on January 27 on a schedule to reopen schools. A plan for secondary schools to return in-person is in place and would be enacted when allowed by Alameda County Public Health Department. Principals from Piedmont High and Middle School, and Millennium High sent out documents, videos and a survey to parents on Monday, February 1 outlining the proposed schedules for in-person learning to resume. Although the agreement is tentative, it was agreed upon in spirit on January 27 by the teachers and the district. “It is not voted upon or finalized, but we want to give parents a heads-up because we feel A proposed schedule for Piedmont High School students would let half of the students on campus each week. When on campus students would meet with periods 1-7 once through the week for 1 hour, 15 minutes. Half of each day would be spent doing distance learning. strongly that we will be able to move forward,” Supt. Booker said in the School Board meeting last week on January 27. A special school board meeting will take place next Monday, February 8 at 6 p.m. for the board to review and approve the schedules. The surveys sent to parents gave high school and middle school parents one week to choose in-person or distance learning for their students. Completed surveys are due back by 9:00 a.m. on Monday, February 8th.

articles.text: Editor: I am an Oakland resident and am writing in support of extending the lease and operation of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. My first time there was for the showing of a movie about a horrible situation on the 57 bus in Oakland. (The 57 Bus: A True Story of Two Teenagers and the Crime That Changed Their Lives) Then I went to the center when they were presenting a “Jazz in the neighborhood” program which introduced me to an intimate setting with great musicians. The volunteers had done a good job with a nice setting and a very welcoming atmosphere. Today, I received a video in commemoration of the liberation of Auschwitz gas chamber camp and was blown away with emotions yet I don’t have a Jewish background. So, for me, the Piedmont Center for the Arts is a place where I can safely see, hear, feel, a different, not commercial, art experience. It’s invaluable. –Elisabeth Heidorn
articles.title: Why I respect the work of the Center for the Arts

articles.text: Editor: May I add my voice to the chorus of community members who are writing in support of the Piedmont Community Arts Center and the renewal of their lease. The Arts Center is one of the most valuable of Piedmont’s many assets. It has become, as currently organized and managed, a wonderful place to hear music, view art and listen to lectures. The entire surrounding community benefits from this jewel of a site and its variety of offerings. Its popularity and ability to attract wonderful performers speaks to the incredible job being done by the current staff of devoted volunteers. As a former Art teacher at Piedmont High School, I only wish it had been available when I was there, as it is providing all students, not just those in a class, a place to pursue and display their art. articles.text: Editor: How is it that we elect all those low-life bad actors as president? No, not him. I mean Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, both Roosevelts, Hoover, and two shot and killed in office, Presidents Garfield and McKinley? The wise souls on the San Francisco School Board are forcing taking all those names off SF schools right away because of their transgressions. This is fact, not fiction. No, I didn’t call it a knee-jerk reaction, nor call the school board members jerks. Also scrubbed are schools named for Padre Junipero Serra who founded most of the early California missions, John Muir, Robert Loius Stevenson and Francis Scott Key of National Anthem fame. Maybe the anthem from F.S. Key could be replaced by some lively number by Michael Jackson? Or can we rename those schools after some of those superstar baseball players who thrived on taking power-enhancing steroids, dismissed as a much lesser sin? Rest assured, California is not a loony bin, though all that sunshine we get here might alter brains and rational thinking. articles.text: Over 250 Piedmonters have been fully vaccinated Piedmont residents have been fully vaccinated against COVID- 19, while 1,143 Piedmonters have received the first of two doses needed for vaccination. Alameda County has administered over 145,000 COVID-19 vaccine doses as of Monday, February 1, according to the California Department of Public Health. The county is now the seventh in the state in terms of total doses administered and has administered more doses than every Bay Area county besides Santa Clara County. However, demand for the vaccine is far outstripping supply – eligible residents have reported waiting on hold for long stretches of time and general confusion about how to sign up for appointments. Last week, the state changed its vaccine distribution plan, but administration varies from county to county due to logistical delays. People 65 years of age and older are eligible for the vaccine, according to the state. Additionally, workers in education, childcare, food, grocery and agriculture sectors are eligible. This group, known as Phase 1B Tier One by the state, includes about 8.5 million Californians. As of press time the Alameda County Public Health Department has not announced that vaccine providers are open for appointments to people in Phase 1B. Instead, the county is still focused on Phase 1A, which includes healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. Phase 1A was the first group eligible for the vaccine when the first doses arrived in December. Phase 1A includes an estimated 3 million people statewide and over 145,000 in Alameda County. The county plans to start vaccinating those in Phase 1B Tier One in the “coming weeks,” according to the ACPHD. Importantly, both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccines that are being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. The county has been administering both Pfizer and Moderna vaccines on pretty equal footing, with about 7 percent more Moderna vaccines being administered than Pfizer. After Phase 1A and Phase 1B Tier One, the next group of people prioritized to receive the vaccine according to the state plan is Phase 1B Tier Two. This group includes workers in transportation, logistics, industrial, commercial, residential, sheltering facilities and critical manufacturing. It also includes people who live in congregate settings, like the incarcerated and the homeless. California’s Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said at a press conference yesterday, Tuesday, February 2 that the state hopes to outline when these groups of people are eligible by next week. Likely, Phase 1B Tier Two will be eligible sometime in the spring. this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. With vaccine supply and the state’s distribution plans in flux, the timetable is subject to change. The state has rapidly ramped up its vaccine distribution. By the end of January, around 180,000 people per day were being vaccinated. The state is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On that website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when their turn is up. The state has administered over 3.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 5.8 million doses, according to the California Department of Public Health. As of press time, 1.5 percent of the state’s population has been fully vaccinated, according to Bloomberg news, while 7.2 percent of Californians have received at least one shot. California is still amongst the worst states in terms of vaccine distribution so far, even though it holds more total doses than any other state. pages.text: Wednesday, February 3, 2021 3 Covid News County still focusing vaccinations on healthcare workers, retirement homes Over 250 Piedmonters have been fully vaccinated By Barry Eitel By the end of January, 255 Piedmont residents have been fully vaccinated against COVID- 19, while 1,143 Piedmonters have received the first of two doses needed for vaccination. Alameda County has administered over 145,000 COVID-19 vaccine doses as of Monday, February 1, according to the California Department of Public Health. The county is now the seventh in the state in terms of total doses administered and has administered more doses than every Bay Area county besides Santa Clara County. However, demand for the vaccine is far outstripping supply – eligible residents have reported waiting on hold for long stretches of time and general confusion about how to sign up for appointments. Last week, the state changed its vaccine distribution plan, but administration varies from county to county due to logistical delays. People 65 years of age and older are eligible for the vaccine, according to the state. Additionally, workers in education, childcare, food, grocery and agriculture sectors are eligible. This group, known as Phase 1B Tier One by the state, includes about 8.5 million Californians. As of press time the Alameda County Public Health Department has not announced that vaccine providers are open for appointments to people in Phase 1B. Instead, the county is still focused on Phase 1A, which includes healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities. Phase 1A was the first group eligible for the vaccine when the first doses arrived in December. Phase 1A includes an estimated 3 million people statewide and over 145,000 in Alameda County. The county plans to start vaccinating those in Phase 1B Tier One in the “coming weeks,” according to the ACPHD. Importantly, both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccines that are being used in California require patients to receive two doses of vaccine administered several weeks apart. The county has been administering both Pfizer and Moderna vaccines on pretty equal footing, with about 7 percent more Moderna vaccines being administered than Pfizer. After Phase 1A and Phase 1B Tier One, the next group of people prioritized to receive the vaccine according to the state plan is Phase 1B Tier Two. This group includes workers in transportation, logistics, industrial, commercial, residential, sheltering facilities and critical manufacturing. It also includes people who live in congregate settings, like the incarcerated and the homeless. California’s Health and Human Services Secretary Mark Ghaly said at a press conference yesterday, Tuesday, February 2 that the state hopes to outline when these groups of people are eligible by next week. Likely, Phase 1B Tier Two will be eligible sometime in the spring. By the summer and fall of this year, anyone who wants to receive a COVID-19 vaccine should be able to receive it, the state believes. With vaccine supply and the state’s distribution plans in flux, the timetable is subject to change. The state has rapidly ramped up its vaccine distribution. By the end of January, around 180,000 people per day were being vaccinated. The state is encouraging residents to utilize a new digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn. ca.gov. On that website, Californians can find out their eligibility and, if eligible, they can schedule a vaccination appointment. Those who are not eligible for vaccination can sign up for notifications when their turn is up. The state has administered over 3.6 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 5.8 million doses, according to the California Department of Public Health. As of press time, 1.5 percent of the state’s population has been fully vaccinated, according to Bloomberg news, while 7.2 percent of Californians have received at least one shot. California is still amongst the worst states in terms of vaccine distribution so far, even though it holds more total doses than any other state. Along with using the My Tool website, the county encourages people 65 years and older to contact their healthcare provider to see if vaccine doses are available to them. articles.text: Congresswoman Barbara Lee of Oakland recently was named the new Chair of the House Appropriations subcommittee on State and Foreign Operations (SFOPS) on January 25. She will be the first African American member of Congress to serve as Chair of the subcommittee. The subcommittee, SFOPS, funds the state department and other foreign operations accounts, and is one of the 12 annual appropriations acts that fund the federal government each fiscal year. “I’m honored to serve as Chair of the Appropriations State and Foreign Operations Subcommittee,” Lee said. “This is a critical time for global investment and cooperation as we fight back a global pandemic, and we have much work to do.” She said that her top priorities on this committee will be investing in diplomacy, foreign assistance, and development programs. “[These] must be at the forefront of our approach, leaving behind the military first approach of the last 4 years. It’s also critical that we reinvest in the State Department and work to ensure our diplomatic corps and all aspects of our international affairs reflect the diversity of the country,” she said. Lee added that the subcommittee must take bold action in tackling the “existential threat of climate change.” She plans on using United Nations sustainable development goals as a guide to address pivotal issues such as global hunger, poverty, education, gender equality, reproductive justice, and economic equality. Lee served on the Foreign Affairs Committee for 10 years and has served on the Appropriations Committee for 14 years. She is also the Co-Chair of the Steering & Policy Committee, a senior member of the Appropriations Committee, former Chair of the Congressional Black Caucus. She also serves as Chair of the Majority Leader’s Task Force on Poverty and Opportunity. “I will lead and legislate as I always have on this committee and my entire career in Congress: through a lens of racial equity, which is needed now more than ever. I’m honored to serve in this critical moment to confront this global pandemic, put America’s priorities at the center of our funding initiatives, while respecting sovereignty of other nations, and help renew our global leadership in the world,” Lee said. In this position, Lee will be following in the footsteps of former officeholder and colleague, Ron Dellums, who was reelected 11 times from the Oakland-based district. Lee began her career in politics by serving as an intern in Dellums’ office – a place she would spend the next decade in service to her East Bay community. Upon Dellums’ retirement in February 1998, Lee was elected to succeed him.
articles.title: Barbara Lee to chair House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee

articles.text: Some Piedmont residents have questioned their neighbors’ lack of compliance to city sign ordinances to remove lawn signs following an election. The city has indicated it sent a reminder of sign ordinances on November 30, 2020. Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed that this followed an extremely high level of participation in recent elections, local and general. “We were looking for people who had put up signs to do their due diligence to remove the signs after the campaigns [had ended]. We added that on the city’s homepage to put the word out that these are the city’s rules,” he said. Current city code requires that all political signs be removed from yards within 10 days following an election. The ordinance does not regulate signs on the basis of content. The effort is mainly concerned with signs posted in yards, in windows, and on walls of residential properties. City Code Division 17.36 requires that only a maximum of 2 signs be allowed, with a maximum height of four feet per sign, including frame. The city of Piedmont will make sure that every resident knows what the rules are,” King said, and added that Piedmont “takes seriously peoples’ right to free speech and is committed to ensuring everyone’s constitutional rights are respected, while clarifying sign regulations.”

articles.text: Piedmont received $2.4 million in 2016 to create plan Piedmont is continuing to explore affordable housing possibilities as a looming December 31 deadline to produce a proposal puts pressure on the city. In an effort to use available funds, Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell told city council members at their meeting on Monday night, February 1, that the city is seeking to extend the deadline by one year. Measure A1 was approved by voters in Alameda County in 2016 to create and preserve more affordable housing throughout the county. Piedmont was advised that year that it would be receiving slightly more than $2 million as an incentive to create and implement a plan. “Currently, we would need a proposal [to create affordable housing] by the end of this year. We’re asked for that deadline to be delayed for one year. That gives us time to put together the right package for Piedmont,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed. A housing element is one of seven elements, or chapters, that the state of California mandates a city or county include in its General Plan. A city’s goals for affordable housing and the measures it intends to take to reach those goals are included in a housing element. The city received $2,431,300 from Measure A-1, and is allowed to follow its own procurement processes to preliminarily select projects for funding. That funding was subsequently reduced to $2.2 million when Alameda County determined that housing developments in Oakland were at risk of failing after changes to the federal corporate tax rate, and money was reallocated from other Alameda County jurisdictions, including Piedmont, to Oakland. Given its existing development with single-family residences, Piedmont has largely relied on the construction of accessory dwelling units (granny flats) to supply new housing units, including those that are rent-restricted or otherwise affordable. The “built-out” characteristic of the city means there is less vacant or otherwise available land to utilize for new housing development than its East Bay neighbors may have. Since 2017, City staff has worked with County staff and Habitat for Humanity East Bay/ Silicon Valley to develop Measure A1 programs for affordable ADUs in Piedmont. To use the Measure A-1 funds, cities must adhere to supportive guidelines; for example, projects must be affordable for 55 years. This makes sense for a multi-family housing development, but less so for ADUs on single-family properties, which tend to change ownership more frequently. The City has asked Alameda County Supervisor Keith Carson to help facilitate a waiver from the Board of Supervisors’ Measure A-1 guidelines that requires Measure A-1 projects to have a 55-year deed restriction for affordability. This effort is still underway, according to Macdonald-Powell. According to Alameda County Housing and Community Development, the 55-year restriction was put in place to encourage long-term affordability. Piedmont’s reason for replacing the five-decade long restriction with a 10-year restriction is because a “shorter affordability term appropriate for single-family dwellings would make the program more marketable and improve its chances of success.” The possibility of “building-up” affordable units in Piedmont was brought up during the public comment portion of Monday’s meeting, and discussed amongst councilmembers. One resident pointed to Albany’s success thus far with affordable housing projects. Piedmont received the least amount of money in Alameda County, with Albany, having received $2,588,918, being the second least. Albany entered into an agreement with Satellite Affordable Housing Associates for the development of a 62-unit project located at 755 Cleveland Avenue, with an estimated completion of August 2022. The cost for the development is $43.8 million. According to Albany Community Development Director Jeff Bond, Albany is, like Piedmont, a built-out city. Piedmont, however, is unique that it is almost entirely builtout with single family homes and has virtually no commerce corridor. “Albany has a sizeable portion [of the city] that is zoned for mixed-use or multi-family units. There are a lot of parcels [in Albany], of significant size, that are zoned for this type of development, whereas Piedmont is overwhelmingly single-family residential with smaller lots,” Jackson said. “The size and availability of sites in Piedmont for the development of mid- to large-sized multi-family apartment buildings are different than in Albany, where the availability of this type of site means they can more quickly find a site as well as a development partner to [execute] that.” On August 17, 2020, Piedmont made the first step toward considering using the Measure A1 projects by entering into a contract with Lisa Wise Consulting to research incentives for the construction of ADUs. Some members of the public at Monday’s meeting questioned whether ADUs are an appropriate size for families. Resident Randy Wu stated that a 400-square-foot ADU he rented out to a Piedmont teacher “was perfect for a single individual” but not a small family, and he urged councilmembers to consider alternatives. Even if Piedmont does not use the allocated funds, they will still go toward affordable housing in Alameda County. Piedmont is not alone in asking for an extension and is not the only city in the county that has yet to use its funds. In addition, city council recommended that the Planning Commission set up an ad hoc subcommittee with the sole purpose of assisting staff and council in developing Measure A1 projects.
articles.title: City asks county for 1 more year to create affordable housing plan

articles.text: Michelle Baack shows off the Mulberry’s Market gift basket that she won in the city’s Climate Challenge Raffle. Join the challenge and do your part on climate challenge at www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org. Last month Michelle Baack got a little help ushering in the new year in the form of “the best raffle prize basket ever” as a reward for taking action on climate change. As the winner of the Piedmont Climate Challenge Raffle organized by the city, Michelle opened her front door to find a basket sitting on her doorstep – a basket filled with wine, cookies, truffles, cocktails and more, all courtesy of Mulberry’s Market. “What a way to ring in 2021,” she wrote in a thank you note. Michelle was recruited to participate in the Piedmont Climate Challenge by her neighbor and friend Claudia Harrison, one of Piedmont Connect’s Climate Challenge ambassadors. “When we joined the Climate Challenge in 2019 we had already done a lot of stuff to address climate change,” Michelle said. The Baacks had bought an older home on Trestle Glen Road, complete with avocado-colored refrigerator, so they had replaced old windows with new double-paned, more energy-efficient models and switched to LED lighting with motion sensors. Michelle and her husband, Jim, already walked to the corner to take the bus or casual carpool to work in San Francisco. Thanks to their close network of neighbors who carpooled for kids’ activities, the Baacks remained a two-car family when their children got their driver’s licenses. Now when her kids come home in the summer, Michelle rents a Zipcar when they are in a pinch. “When we travel to other cities, we use Zipcar too, so we don’t tie up a rental car for the whole time, hoping that means fewer cars overall,” Michelle said. But since COVID hit, the Baacks have been doing even more to reduce their environmental footprints. “We buy a lot more locally,” she said. When she does order from Amazon, she consolidates the order to be delivered on a certain day to reduce transportation emissions. They also have cut down on their waste. Michelle is buying food from Zero Grocery in Berkeley, the first plastic-free grocery delivery service. “My husband and I have a tiny bag of garbage after one week,” she quipped. She said she has been struck by how different attitudes and practices are in the Midwest, where her kids now live. “There is less focus on recycling in the Midwest, and what you can put in recycling bins is more limited,” she said. “There are no options for recycling plastic bags and wrappers, which our kids learned about at Havens with ‘baggy blue’ recycling.” She also observed that most apartment buildings in the Midwest don’t have compost service, either. “To-go food is mostly packaged in plastic or Styrofoam, not in compostable options that we see in the Bay Area,” Michelle said. “Here in Piedmont, we take it for granted that we can recycle so much and compost and have almost no real ‘garbage’ in our bin every week.” If you haven’t joined the Piedmont Climate Challenge yet, check it out at www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org.
articles.title: Piedmont Climate Challenge Raffle – and the winner is… Michelle Baack

By Ronna Kelly Last month Michelle Baack got a little help ushering in the new year in the form of “the best raffle prize basket ever” as a reward for taking action on climate change. As the winner of the Piedmont Climate Challenge Raffle organized by the city, Michelle opened her front door to find a basket sitting on her doorstep – a basket filled with wine, cookies, truffles, cocktails and more, all courtesy of Mulberry’s Market. “What a way to ring in 2021,” she wrote in a thank you note. Michelle was recruited to participate in the Piedmont Climate Challenge by her neighbor and friend Claudia Harrison, one of Piedmont Connect’s Climate Challenge ambassadors. “When we joined the Climate Challenge in 2019 we had already done a lot of stuff to address climate change,” Michelle said. The Baacks had bought an older home on Trestle Glen Road, complete with avocado-colored refrigerator, so they had replaced old windows with new double-paned, more energy-efficient models and switched to LED lighting with motion sensors. Michelle and her husband, Jim, already walked to the corner to take the bus or casual carpool to work in San Francisco. Thanks to their close network of neighbors who carpooled for kids’ activities, the Baacks remained a two-car family when their children got their driver’s licenses. Now when her kids come home in the summer, Michelle rents a Zipcar when they are in a pinch. “When we travel to other cities, we use Zipcar too, so we don’t tie up a rental car for the whole time, hoping that means fewer cars overall,” Michelle said. But since COVID hit, the Baacks have been doing even more to reduce their environmental footprints. “We buy a lot more locally,” she said. When she does order from Amazon, she consolidates the order to be delivered on a certain day to reduce transportation emissions. They also have cut down on their waste. Michelle is buying food from Zero Grocery in Berkeley, the first plastic-free grocery delivery service. “My husband and I have a tiny bag of garbage after one week,” she quipped. She said she has been struck by how different attitudes and practices are in the Midwest, where her kids now live. “There is less focus on recycling in the Midwest, and what you can put in recycling bins is more limited,” she said. “There are no options for recycling plastic bags and wrappers, which our kids learned about at Havens with ‘baggy blue’ recycling.” She also observed that most apartment buildings in the Midwest don’t have compost service, either. “To-go food is mostly packaged in plastic or Styrofoam, not in compostable options that we see in the Bay Area,” Michelle said. “Here in Piedmont, we take it for granted that we can recycle so much and compost and have almost no real ‘garbage’ in our bin every week.” If you haven’t joined the Piedmont Climate Challenge yet, check it out at www.piedmontclimatechallenge.org. City asks county for 1 more year to create affordable housing plan Piedmont received $2.4 million in 2016 to create plan By Allyson Aleksey Piedmont is continuing to explore affordable housing possibilities as a looming December 31 deadline to produce a proposal puts pressure on the city. In an effort to use available funds, Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell told city council members at their meeting on Monday night, February 1, that the city is seeking to extend the deadline by one year. Measure A1 was approved by voters in Alameda County in 2016 to create and preserve more affordable housing throughout the county. Piedmont was advised that year that it would be receiving slightly more than $2 million as an incentive to create and implement a plan. “Currently, we would need a proposal [to create affordable housing] by the end of this year. We’re asked for that deadline to be delayed for one year. That gives us time to put together the right package for Piedmont,” Planning Director Kevin Jackson confirmed. A housing element is one of seven elements, or chapters, that the state of California mandates a city or county include in its General Plan. A city’s goals for affordable housing and the measures it intends to take to reach those goals are included in a housing element. The city received $2,431,300 from Measure A-1, and is allowed to follow its own procurement processes to preliminarily select projects for funding. That funding was subsequently reduced to $2.2 million when Alameda County determined that housing developments in Oakland were at risk of failing after changes to the federal corporate tax rate, and money was reallocated from other Alameda County jurisdictions, including Piedmont, to Oakland. Given its existing development with single-family residences, Piedmont has largely relied on the construction of accessory dwelling units (granny flats) to supply new housing units, including those that are rent-restricted or otherwise affordable. The “built-out” characteristic of the city means there is less vacant or otherwise available land to utilize for new housing development than its East Bay neighbors may have. Since 2017, City staff has worked with County staff and Habitat for Humanity East Bay/ Silicon Valley to develop Measure A1 programs for affordable ADUs in Piedmont. To use the Measure A-1 funds, cities must adhere to supportive guidelines; for example, projects must be affordable for 55 years. This makes sense for a multi-family housing development, but less so for ADUs on single-family properties, which tend to change ownership more frequently. The City has asked Alameda County Supervisor Keith Carson to help facilitate a waiver from the Board of Supervisors’ Measure A-1 guidelines that requires Measure A-1 projects to have a 55-year deed restriction for affordability. This effort is still underway, according to Macdonald-Powell. According to Alameda County Housing and Community Development, the 55-year restriction was put in place to encourage long-term affordability. Piedmont’s reason for replacing the five-decade long restriction with a 10-year restriction is because a “shorter affordability term appropriate for single-family dwellings would make the program more marketable and improve its chances of success.” The possibility of “building-up” affordable units in Piedmont was brought up during the public comment portion of Monday’s meeting, and discussed amongst councilmembers. One resident pointed to Albany’s success thus far with affordable housing projects. Piedmont received the least amount of money in Alameda County, with Albany, having received $2,588,918, being the second least. Albany entered into an agreement with Satellite Affordable Housing Associates for the development of a 62-unit project located at 755 Cleveland Avenue, with an estimated completion of August 2022. The cost for the development is $43.8 million. According to Albany Community Development Director Jeff Bond, Albany is, like Piedmont, a built-out city. Piedmont, however, is unique that it is almost entirely builtout with single family homes and has virtually no commerce corridor. “Albany has a sizeable portion [of the city] that is zoned for mixed-use or multi-family units. There are a lot of parcels [in Albany], of significant size, that are zoned for this type of development, whereas Piedmont is overwhelmingly single-family residential with smaller lots,” Jackson said. “The size and availability of sites in Piedmont for the development of mid- to large-sized multi-family apartment buildings are different than in Albany, where the availability of this type of site means they can more quickly find a site as well as a development partner to [execute] that.” On August 17, 2020, Piedmont made the first step toward considering using the Measure A1 projects by entering into a contract with Lisa Wise Consulting to research incentives for the construction of ADUs. Some members of the public at Monday’s meeting questioned whether ADUs are an appropriate size for families. Resident Randy Wu stated that a 400-square-foot ADU he rented out to a Piedmont teacher “was perfect for a single individual” but not a small family, and he urged councilmembers to consider alternatives. Even if Piedmont does not use the allocated funds, they will still go toward affordable housing in Alameda County. Piedmont is not alone in asking for an extension and is not the only city in the county that has yet to use its funds. In addition, city council recommended that the Planning Commission set up an ad hoc subcommittee with the sole purpose of assisting staff and council in developing Measure A1 projects. articles.text: For the creative soul, inspiration can come from anywhere. When Athena Chang needed an idea for a high school art project, she found it in her pocket — and a way to highlight racial prejudice. “I really didn’t know what I was going to do,” said the 17-yearold senior. “But I was wearing this jacket with a mask in the pocket. I was playing with the mask, and I was thinking, ‘This is the most pertinent thing right now.’ And it all sort of came to me.” A face mask, so commonplace during the COVID-19 pandemic, was also a symbol of suppression, Chang said, and she turned that idea into a multi-media project for her Advanced Placement Art class at Piedmont High School. “When you’re wearing a mask, your voice is kind of muffled, and I think that’s what is happening to the Asian-American community a little bit,” said Chang. “The project is about restoring voice to the people who have sort of lost it.” Chang asked local AsianAmerican students for photos of themselves wearing masks. She also interviewed them about their own experiences during the pandemic. “Everybody was pretty open about their feelings,” she said. “I think people want to be open PHS Senior Athena Chang about it. They see the value of putting minority voices out there.” Now Chang is combining the visual and audio elements to create an immersive experience that she plans to launch online, and pandemic-permitting in a physical installation this spring. A lifelong artist, she hopes her project will help to change how people think about race and prejudice in America. “When you grow up as a person of color in this country, you know that you’ll be treated as lesser than,” Chang said. “This could be the time for that change to come.” Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for students in Piedmont schools.
articles.title: Student artist takes on challenge of racism

articles.text: Workshops to be held Feb.10, 12 for all high school students The high school student group Piedmont for Consent will lead a workshop for all 2nd period classes at Piedmont and Millennium High on Wednesday and Friday, February 10 and 12. Second period classes will begin at 9:00 a.m. Students will either watch the Consent Workshop with their classmates or attend office hours. The Consent Workshop includes information about consent, boundaries, communication, physiological defense responses to stressful situations, unhealthy behaviors, alcohol and other drugs, reporting, and resources for everyone to continue the discussion and to get help. A parent workshop will be held two days prior on Monday, February 8 at 7:00 p.m. on Zoom to preview the content that the students will be discussing in the workshop that week. Piedmont For Consent is a group that formed in response to the Piedmont Protectors Instagram Account last summer. Co-Presidents Kaeli Huh and Anna Gotto, along with faculty mentor Kimberly Taylor, have led the group in conversations and education about consent throughout the fall and winter. They created the Consent Workshop when it was determined that the annual Consent Assembly was not adaptable to an online setting. It is hoped that this workshop will be a yearly addition to the Consent Assembly when it returns in person, as well as the start of this year’s Consent Education for the Piedmont community. In addition, the Piedmont for Consent group will host a discussion and debriefing of the workshop for all interested students in their weekly meeting on Thursday, February 25 from 3:15-4:30 p.m. For more information, contact Kimberly Taylor, PHS/PMS Acting and Drama Teacher and Mentor to Piedmont for Consent, at (ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us), or co-Presidents Kaeli Huh (22kaelihu@piedmont.k12.ca.us) and Anna Gotto (23annago@ piedmont.k12.ca.us).

articles.text: With Valentine’s Day around the corner, I have fond memories of time spent at my childhood elementary school decorating a white valentine bag and placing it on my desk for hand deliveries from my classmates. At home, I made individual valentine cards, folded them and then carefully inserted the finished card into an envelope. I addressed the envelope in my best handwriting while being certain to correctly copy the spelling from the class list. It was a much- loved tradition and one that has been carried over to this day at elementary schools everywhere. Occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! For those who know me well, they may think that it’s the candy conversation of hearts and chocolates. Though the candies are a plus, OT’s love Valentine’s Day for Do It Yourself (DIY) valentine cards. One DIY valentine card encompasses drawing, coloring, folding, cutting with scissors, gluing and handwriting. It’s an OT’s dream come true. It’s a simple arts and crafts activity that includes the many necessary functional fine motor skills that a student needs in order to participate and be successful at school. More specifically, these fine motor activities require fine motor precision, a variety of grasp patterns, bilateral coordination and eye-hand coordination. But wait, there’s even more... A Valentine is more than a nice thought. One DIY valentine card also supports: • Visual Perception. For example, placement/centering written messages or designs. • Visual Motor Integration to draw heart designs. • Visual Skills for near point copying an address to an envelope. • Executive function for task initiation, sustained attention, planning and organization for a finished product. • Life skills (addressing an envelope.) • Creativity • Self esteem Whew! That’s a lot of skills for one Valentine’s Day card. You can certainly see why occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! So, this year join occupational therapists everywhere and their love of Valentine’s Day by opting out of store-bought cards in favor of DIY. Since traditional in-class deliveries are not possible, take the opportunity for a movement break and walk to the nearby mailbox, or even hand-deliver cards to your friends’ doorsteps. Kimberly Bonacum, MS, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional information, contact mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com.
articles.title: Thinking Outside The Classroom Homemade Valentine cards much more than expression of love

articles.text: Let me start off by saying that it’s a miracle that I have made it this far in quarantine. For all the older siblings and parents reading, you will never feel our pain, but please continue reading. For the past 10 months I have been living with a sister who is graduating from high school, so all I ever hear about is college applications, and whether the college has released its decision. So, when life goes back to normal and I am out and about and trying to make small talk, all I talk about is how to apply to colleges and why a 12-point font is necessary when writing to Big 10 schools. Every day when I sit down for dinner, I am praying that maybe something – anything – would have happened so I won’t have to listen to what I now call “College Talk With The Vackers.” We talk about the acceptance rates, who is getting into which college and who isn’t, and when the next deadline will be. On top all of that, when I suggest that we might want to change the topic, everyone says, “Well then, what do you want to talk about?” It’s at that point that my mind just goes blank. It’s as if I suddenly have forgotten every talkable topic on Earth. In defeat I go back to eating my food and listening to the debate about whatever essay my sister has to finish. The next part of being a younger sibling is having to deal with the general older sibling stuff. Obviously, we last-borns had to deal with our older sisters or brothers in the pre-COVID-19 world, but now that we are in close quarters, there’s no escape. So, we have to resort to drastic measures, like saying, “Hello! Your lesser counterpart is talking. Can you please pay attention to us every once in a while? Like, Yoo-hoo. Will you take a break and maybe even talk to me. After all, I am not simply white noise.” Yes, I know you have a boyfriend, but why not also pay attention to the miracle of a sibling your parents gave you? “And another thing, please stop acting like a parent when the real parents aren’t around: it drives us crazy.” One time I was minding my own business and my sister seemed to just materialize out of nowhere, scaring the living daylights out of me. The next thing I know I’m being ordered to brush my hair, eat lunch, wear a mask, put on a jacket instead of a vest… and so on. Each time I say I am going to take a shower, my sister turns into Usain Bolt and sprints by me and inside the bathroom. Would an adult really do that? But I have to say that being younger has some perks. We actually get away with everything. I once got an “F” three times in a row on a math test and nobody batted an eyelash. My sister, on the other hand, once got a “C” and almost went into orbit. Younger siblings can get something as minor as a paper cut but get to be exempt from school for the rest of the year. Older siblings have to soldier on and go to school with a 100-degree fever. If we wanted to get takeout or watch a movie, mountains would be moved to make it happen. Let’s talk about curfew. It goes like this: eldest, 10 p.m. sharp or they’re grounded. Middle child, midnight or 1 a.m. Last but certainly not least, the youngest gets a curfew of 5 to 7 business days. We get the most love and attention, even though the parents claim they don’t have a favorite. And so, although most of the time we are overlooked by our siblings, we still know we hold the supreme position in the family. And despite what we have to endure from our older siblings, we do love them. One day in the near future when my sister goes off to start a new chapter at whatever college she attends, I will shed some tears, because I lost my partner in crime. Things won’t be the same without my second mom…oops, I mean my sister. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.
articles.title: CRYSTAL’S REFLECTIONS Life of a younger sibling in quarantine

For example, placement/centering written messages or designs. • Visual Motor Integration to draw heart designs. • Visual Skills for near point copying an address to an envelope. • Executive function for task initiation, sustained attention, planning and organization for a finished product. • Life skills (addressing an envelope.) • Creativity • Self esteem Whew! That’s a lot of skills for one Valentine’s Day card. You can certainly see why occupational therapists love Valentine’s Day! So, this year join occupational therapists everywhere and their love of Valentine’s Day by opting out of store-bought cards in favor of DIY. Since traditional in-class deliveries are not possible, take the opportunity for a movement break and walk to the nearby mailbox, or even hand-deliver cards to your friends’ doorsteps. Kimberly Bonacum, MS, OTR/L, is an occupational therapist for Piedmont Unified School District and owner of Mindful Fidgets, LLC www.mindfulfidgets.com. For additional information, contact mindfulfidgets@ gmail.com. CRYSTAL’S REFLECTIONS Life of a younger sibling in quarantine By Crystal Vacker Let me start off by saying that it’s a miracle that I have made it this far in quarantine. For all the older siblings and parents reading, you will never feel our pain, but please continue reading. For the past 10 months I have been living with a sister who is graduating from high school, so all I ever hear about is college applications, and whether the college has released its decision. So, when life goes back to normal and I am out and about and trying to make small talk, all I talk about is how to apply to colleges and why a 12-point font is necessary when writing to Big 10 schools. Every day when I sit down for dinner, I am praying that maybe something – anything – would have happened so I won’t have to listen to what I now call “College Talk With The Vackers.” We talk about the acceptance rates, who is getting into which college and who isn’t, and when the next deadline will be. On top all of that, when I suggest that we might want to change the topic, everyone says, “Well then, what do you want to talk about?” It’s at that point that my mind just goes blank. It’s as if I suddenly have forgotten every talkable topic on Earth. In defeat I go back to eating my food and listening to the debate about whatever essay my sister has to finish. The next part of being a younger sibling is having to deal with the general older sibling stuff. Obviously, we last-borns had to deal with our older sisters or brothers in the pre-COVID-19 world, but now that we are in close quarters, there’s no escape. So, we have to resort to drastic measures, like saying, “Hello! Your lesser counterpart is talking. Can you please pay attention to us every once in a while? Like, Yoo-hoo. Will you take a break and maybe even talk to me. After all, I am not simply white noise.” Yes, I know you have a boyfriend, but why not also pay attention to the miracle of a sibling your parents gave you? “And another thing, please stop acting like a parent when the real parents aren’t around: it drives us crazy.” One time I was minding my own business and my sister seemed to just materialize out of nowhere, scaring the living daylights out of me. The next thing I know I’m being ordered to brush my hair, eat lunch, wear a mask, put on a jacket instead of a vest… and so on. Each time I say I am going to take a shower, my sister turns into Usain Bolt and sprints by me and inside the bathroom. Would an adult really do that? But I have to say that being younger has some perks. We actually get away with everything. I once got an “F” three times in a row on a math test and nobody batted an eyelash. My sister, on the other hand, once got a “C” and almost went into orbit. Younger siblings can get something as minor as a paper cut but get to be exempt from school for the rest of the year. Older siblings have to soldier on and go to school with a 100-degree fever. If we wanted to get takeout or watch a movie, mountains would be moved to make it happen. Let’s talk about curfew. It goes like this: eldest, 10 p.m. sharp or they’re grounded. Middle child, midnight or 1 a.m. Last but certainly not least, the youngest gets a curfew of 5 to 7 business days. We get the most love and attention, even though the parents claim they don’t have a favorite. And so, although most of the time we are overlooked by our siblings, we still know we hold the supreme position in the family. And despite what we have to endure from our older siblings, we do love them. One day in the near future when my sister goes off to start a new chapter at whatever college she attends, I will shed some tears, because I lost my partner in crime. Things won’t be the same without my second mom…oops, I mean my sister. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont student with a keen eye and the ability to be in several places at one time.

articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted. The deadline for nominations is March 15, 2021. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who will be recognized at the May 12 Board of Education meeting. The honoree also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the Board. The award is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered their efforts over a period of time and made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. The first winner in 1998 was Hunter McCreary, founder of PLOT (Piedmont Light Opera Theatre). Last year’s winner was Sue Smegal, a former teacher, school board member, and longtime active supporter of Piedmont schools. Art Hecht, a former school board member, was a tireless community volunteer dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He served on Piedmont’s Board of Education from 1970 to 1978 and was a champion of Piedmont Continuation High School, the forerunner of Millennium High. The Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by former school board president Dewey Watson in 1998 to honor the legacy of Mr. Hecht. Nomination forms are available on the PUSD website and in the school district office, 760 Magnolia Avenue.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2021. articles.text: The Columbus Zoo and Aquarium, now the permanent home of three orphaned mountain cubs rescued by Cal Fire firefighters last year and brought to the Oakland Zoo, has introduced their resident cougar Jessie to the brood. The three mountain lions were rescued from the devastating Zogg and August Complex fires that burned near Redding in September 2020. The severely burned orphaned male mountain lion cub, named Captain Cal after the firefighters that rescued him, fully recovered 47 days after he was first rushed to Oakland Zoo’s veterinary hospital by the California Department of Fish & Wildlife. With surgery, antibiotics, supportive fluids, pain medication, hand feedings, daily bandage changes, and round-the-clock care, Captain Cal survived and was ready to make the journey last November to his new home at the zoo in Columbus, Ohio. While still at the Oakland Zoo, Captain Cal was joined by two unrelated female cubs, also orphaned by the California wildfires and rehabilitated by Oakland Zoo’s veterinary team. Oakland Zoo documented Cal’s recovery and his bond with his new sisters. The litter of three quickly became “internet famous,” and a tiny but powerful reminder of the consequences of climate change. Columbus Zoo staff were given the honor of naming the two orphaned females – which they named Goldie and Poppy, as an homage to their California origin – home of the Golden poppies. Columbus Zoo kept its promise of introducing an older cougar to the young cubs. Because the three were orphaned at such a young age, they lack the skills most adult mountain lions develop; in their native range, mountain lion cubs stay with their mother until they are about two years old. After exploring their new habitat in the Columbus Zoo’s North America region, Goldie, Captain Cal and Poppy were introduced to the Zoo’s resident adult female cougar, Jessie, who is mostly blind. Zookeepers provided an opportunity for both Jessie and the cubs to explore each other’s spaces, giving them the chance to get familiar with each other. Columbus Zoo staff have observed that Goldie has proven to be the boldest, and saw her approach Jessie several times to paw at her playfully. Her sister Poppy was never far behind. Captain Cal could often be seen shyly peering out at Jessie from behind a Spruce tree while she napped in her den. “Jessie has never been a surrogate mother, but she is doing an amazing job so far,” a Columbus Zoo Facebook post stated. articles.text: Scouts in Piedmont Troop 11 hiked from Stinson Beach to Muir Woods and back on a sunny Saturday in late January. Altogether it was a hike of 12 miles and over 3,000 feet in elevation. “My favorite part was walking through the Steep Ravine Trail and walking along the creek,” said Scout Gus Leonard. “It was really steep, and you could see a lot of stuff.” “I liked finding and looking at the fungi along the trail,” said Pierce Tindle. “My favorite part was the hiking!” said Shayna Chau. The hike started out on the Dipsea Trail, well known for the annual Dipsea Race. After enjoying a break for food and water at Muir Woods National Park, the troop started towards Stinson on the Ben Johnson Trail. This connected with the Stapleveldt Trail, which dropped into the Steep Ravine Trail before reconnecting with the Dipsea. “The views along the Dipsea are beautiful and the second half of the hike is stunning,” said Scoutmaster Tom Smegal. All the Scouts were glad they completed the strenuous hike. Scouts Will Myers and Kajsa Benson said, “Our favorite part was when we were done!” The troop took many measures to remain in line with social distancing requirements. Scouts, parents, and volunteers traveled and ate in family groups. The troop split into two hiking parties of less than 14 people each at the trailhead and staggered the time of their start. Everyone remained masked up throughout the hike, and they spaced out even further when they ate and took water breaks. “It’s been hard to keep the program going during COVID,” confirmed Smegal. “We haven’t been able to do many campouts, and we’re mostly limited to virtual meetings and day trips like this. It’s nice to have an adventure that gives us a chance to see each other in 3D and help the Scouts work on their advancement.” Troop 11 is one of five troops in the Piedmont Council Scouts BSA program. Piedmont’s Scouting program is designed for boys and girls ages 11-17, and focuses on character, fitness, life skills and leadership skills. Families interested in learning more about Piedmont Scouts are encouraged to call Kate Benson, Scout Executive, at 547-4493, or e-mail: contact@piedmontbsa.org. Scout Pierce Tindle shows some fungi found on the hike. Will Sprague and Asst, Scoutmaster Anne Hauss checking the route. Scouts in the younger group paused for a group photo by the Muir Woods sign: Shayna Chau (left), Kajsa Benson, Pierce Tindle, Gus Leonard, Eric Venner, and Will Myers.

articles.text: This is the week leading to Super Bowl Sunday, where the Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers square off for the 55th edition of the America’s biggest sports attraction. Last year’s MVP, QB Patrick Mahomes, and KC could become back-to-back champions, but Tom Brady, a living legend, and the Buccaneers look to spoil the favorites. Here’s a look at this week’s game, and why The Post is selecting the Chiefs to win, despite the Buccaneers being the team to host and play in the Super Bowl. It starts on offense for Kansas City, with quarterback Patrick Mahomes, receiver Tyreek Hill and tight end Travis Kelce. Add to the mix head coach Andy Reid and coordinator Eric Bieniemy’s stellar play-calling, and an ability to grind out close yards with running backs Clyde Edwards-Helaire and Le’Veon Bell, we would have to say that Buccaneers’ defensive coordinator Todd Bowles is going to have his hands full. Lining up the Buc’s potential defense against KC’s superstars leave some predictable holes. Tampa Bay’s top cornerback, Jamel Dean, will likely square up on Hill, while TB may be required to double up on Kelce with a safety and linebacker Lavonte David, who is among the best coverage linebackers in the league. This could leave Tampa susceptible to veteran WR Sammy Watkins, rookie speedster Mecole Hardman, or plays out of the backfield to Edwards-Helaire and Bell. For the Buccaneers and Brady to pull off the upset, they will need major contributions from the receiving core of Mike Evans, Chris Godwin, Antonio Brown, while Brady enacts his Super Bowl magic. Head coach Bruce Arians and Brady could deploy a spread offense with its wideouts to thin out KC’s defensive backfield and lessen the blow of the Chiefs’ already weak pass rush. Tampa struggled mightily in the NFC Championship game against the pass rush with the Packers and likely wants to avoid that again. Furthermore, the Bucs could reap the benefit of LT Eric Fisher being hobbled with an Achilles injury. He’s currently ruled out from the Super Bowl and did not participate in any practice last week. Tampa Bay had five sacks against Green Bay. The Chiefs are currently favored by three-points, a reflection of their Week 12 narrow Photo courtesy of Sporting News The Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers square off for Super Bowl 55 in Tampa Bay, Florida. Photo courtesy of Eurosport Juventus’ Weston McKennie is a 22-year-old American star in Italy’s Serie A. In the photo he scores with a scissor-kick off the volley against Bologna. Photo courtesy of the Star Tribune The Warriors and Stephen Curry look ahead to February with four winnable games coming up against Dallas and San Antonio. 27-24 victory. We’ll go with the Chiefs and a one-possession ballgame: 31-27. Warriors fighting for playoff spot It’s past midway through the NBA season with the Warriors clinging to a No. 7 seed in the Western Conference standings. The Dubs faced a difficult game with the Boston Celtics last night but look ahead to four winnable games over the next week. Some unfortunate news arose on Monday with rookie center James Wiseman sustaining a wrist injury that will force him to miss at least 10 days. The Warriors play back-toback games in Texas against the No. 13 Dallas Mavericks tomorrow and February 6, followed by the No. 10 San Antonio Spurs on Monday and Tuesday, February 8-9. Golden State has not won more than two-games in a row this season in 21 games, so now would be the time to get its first winning streak of 2021 started with the hopes of earning a playoff spot. Weston McKennie making noise in Italy Typically, we reserve the final section of our Pro Sports write-up for England’s Premier League. But this week we want our sports readers to know about U,S, star midfielder Weston McKennie. He is quickly becoming one of the most influential players in the ultra-talented Serie A of Italy. McKennie, 22, signed with Italian superclub Juventus to play alongside Cristiano Ronaldo. Currently on loan from Germany’s Schalke, he made 75 appearances for the German club and scored four goals. His one-year loan contract will likely become a permanent deal due to performance incentives. In just 15 appearances with Juve, he’s already scored three goals, including a beautiful scissor kick goal in a 3-0 win over Barcelona in Champions League on December 8. Following McKennie’s most recent header goal against Bologna on Jan. 24, the youngster is quickly earning the nickname “Wizard Weston” and “Magic McKennie” after his celebration mimicked a wizard casting a spell. After the game, he revealed he’s an enormous fan of Harry Potter. pages.text: Wednesday, February 3, 2021 13 Pro Sports Super Bowl on Sunday; Warriors update, Weston McKennie a U.S. star in Italy By Jonathan Comeaux This is the week leading to Super Bowl Sunday, where the Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers square off for the 55th edition of the America’s biggest sports attraction. Last year’s MVP, QB Patrick Mahomes, and KC could become back-to-back champions, but Tom Brady, a living legend, and the Buccaneers look to spoil the favorites. Here’s a look at this week’s game, and why The Post is selecting the Chiefs to win, despite the Buccaneers being the team to host and play in the Super Bowl. It starts on offense for Kansas City, with quarterback Patrick Mahomes, receiver Tyreek Hill and tight end Travis Kelce. Add to the mix head coach Andy Reid and coordinator Eric Bieniemy’s stellar play-calling, and an ability to grind out close yards with running backs Clyde Edwards-Helaire and Le’Veon Bell, we would have to say that Buccaneers’ defensive coordinator Todd Bowles is going to have his hands full. Lining up the Buc’s potential defense against KC’s superstars leave some predictable holes. Tampa Bay’s top cornerback, Jamel Dean, will likely square up on Hill, while TB may be required to double up on Kelce with a safety and linebacker Lavonte David, who is among the best coverage linebackers in the league. This could leave Tampa susceptible to veteran WR Sammy Watkins, rookie speedster Mecole Hardman, or plays out of the backfield to Edwards-Helaire and Bell. For the Buccaneers and Brady to pull off the upset, they will need major contributions from the receiving core of Mike Evans, Chris Godwin, Antonio Brown, while Brady enacts his Super Bowl magic. Head coach Bruce Arians and Brady could deploy a spread offense with its wideouts to thin out KC’s defensive backfield and lessen the blow of the Chiefs’ already weak pass rush. Tampa struggled mightily in the NFC Championship game against the pass rush with the Packers and likely wants to avoid that again. Furthermore, the Bucs could reap the benefit of LT Eric Fisher being hobbled with an Achilles injury. He’s currently ruled out from the Super Bowl and did not participate in any practice last week. Tampa Bay had five sacks against Green Bay. The Chiefs are currently favored by three-points, a reflection of their Week 12 narrow Photo courtesy of Sporting News The Kansas City Chiefs and Tampa Bay Buccaneers square off for Super Bowl 55 in Tampa Bay, Florida. Photo courtesy of Eurosport Juventus’ Weston McKennie is a 22-year-old American star in Italy’s Serie A. In the photo he scores with a scissor-kick off the volley against Bologna. Photo courtesy of the Star Tribune The Warriors and Stephen Curry look ahead to February with four winnable games coming up against Dallas and San Antonio. 27-24 victory. We’ll go with the Chiefs and a one-possession ballgame: 31-27. Warriors fighting for playoff spot It’s past midway through the NBA season with the Warriors clinging to a No. 7 seed in the Western Conference standings. The Dubs faced a difficult game with the Boston Celtics last night but look ahead to four winnable games over the next week. Some unfortunate news arose on Monday with rookie center James Wiseman sustaining a wrist injury that will force him to miss at least 10 days. The Warriors play back-toback games in Texas against the No. 13 Dallas Mavericks tomorrow and February 6, followed by the No. 10 San Antonio Spurs on Monday and Tuesday, February 8-9. Golden State has not won more than two-games in a row this season in 21 games, so now would be the time to get its first winning streak of 2021 started with the hopes of earning a playoff spot. Weston McKennie making noise in Italy Typically, we reserve the final section of our Pro Sports write-up for England’s Premier League. But this week we want our sports readers to know about U,S, star midfielder Weston McKennie. He is quickly becoming one of the most influential players in the ultra-talented Serie A of Italy. McKennie, 22, signed with Italian superclub Juventus to play alongside Cristiano Ronaldo. Currently on loan from Germany’s Schalke, he made 75 appearances for the German club and scored four goals. His one-year loan contract will likely become a permanent deal due to performance incentives. In just 15 appearances with Juve, he’s already scored three goals, including a beautiful scissor kick goal in a 3-0 win over Barcelona in Champions League on December 8. Following McKennie’s most recent header goal against Bologna on Jan. 24, the youngster is quickly earning the nickname “Wizard Weston” and “Magic McKennie” after his celebration mimicked a wizard casting a spell. After the game, he revealed he’s an enormous fan of Harry Potter. To quote Hagrid from the famed series, “You’re a wizard, Weston!” Marque Premier League match to watch Back to England, some key matches to watch over the next week include Tottenham vs. Chelsea (Feb. 4, 12 p.m.); Manchester United vs. Everton (Feb. 6, 12 p.m.); Liverpool vs. Manchester City (Feb. 7, 8:30 a.m.). articles.text: Firefall at Horsetail Fall starts in two weeks Yosemite National Park re-opened on Monday, February 1 after the recent snow and windstorm pushed through the area, but with some noteworthy adjustments. Lodging and camping is permitted at select locations, but day trips will require advance reservation before visiting. Most of the park is open, but the recent windstorm toppled at least 15 giant Sequoia trees and has caused the park entrance on Highway 41 to be closed, including the Wawona, Badger Pass, Tunnel View and Mariposa Grove areas. Visitors can book reservations online at Recreation.gov between February 8-28, and reservations are already filling up fast. Dayuse reservations are valid from 5 a.m. to 11 p.m. “Day use visitors who arrive by private vehicle or motorcycle must have a day use reservation. Day-use reservations are valid for seven consecutive days and must be validated on the first day that your reservation is scheduled to begin. Visitors arriving on foot or bicycle do not require a day use Photo courtesy of the LA Times Yosemite National Park reopened on February 1 with some lodging available. Starting February 8, the park will require day-use reservations. reservation,” the park advises. Reservations are valid for a full week and must be validated on the scheduled first day of your reservation, otherwise it will be canceled. But dates are already filling up, especially in the middle of the month. Yosemite’s plan coincides with the annual Firefall that is seen at Horsetail Falls between February 11-27. It is a natural phenomenon created when the setting sun reflects off Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. Photo courtesy of Aaronmphotography.com Here is a handy list of the best viewing times for the Firefall at Horsetail Falls in Yosemite Park. Lodging inside the park automatically registers your weeklong reservation. Reservations are currently available at the Yosemite Valley Lodge and The Ahwahnee Hotel. Private lodging is also listed at Wawona, Yosemite West, and Foresta. Camping is only available at the Upper Pines Campground. The annual Firefall of Horsetail Falls is expected to occur between February 11-27.

articles.text: Bay Area sports fans were saddened last week to learn of the passing of legendary public address announcer Dick Callahan. He died on January 29 at age 80. He was the former announcer and voice of the Oakland A’s baseball team, Golden State Warriors basketball team, and the University of California football team. He passed on Friday, January 29. “The Oakland A’s are heartbroken to learn that Dick Callahan passed away this morning. He lent his warm and welcoming voice to the Oakland faithful as our public address announcer for 15 seasons and more than 1,000 games at the Oakland Coliseum. We have lost a beloved member of our family who was a great friend to all who knew him. His passion and love for the A’s was like no other and his impact will never be forgotten. We extend our condolences to Dick’s family and friends during this time,” wrote the A’s in an official statement. Callahan took over PA duties in 2005 after his predecessor, Roy Steele, developed a rare illness. They were big shoes to fill, as A’s fans recalled Steele as the “Voice of God.” Since 2005, Callahan filled in perfectly for Steele, providing visitors to the Oakland Coliseum his enthusiastic voice in pre-game and mid-game announcements and player introductions as they stepped into the batters’ box. “He had a great voice,” said Ken Korach, A’s play-by-play broadcaster since 1980. “It was deep and it was resonant and he spoke with authority. He had a tough assignment to come in after Roy Steele and yet he did it in his own way. He didn’t try to be Roy. He just did a great job and he did it with enthusiasm.” In July Callahan chose to sit out the 2020 season due to health concerns. He had worked at least 1,000 A’s home games over his career. Callahan hit the millennium mark of 1,000 games in the game on May 7, 2019 when A’s pitcher Mike Fiers threw a no-hitter. He also called Dallas Braden’s perfect game in 2010 and Sean Manaea’s no-hitter the most memorable games of his career. “I’m still a little kid from the coal region of Pennsylvania who got lucky,” Callahan said of his 1,000th appearance to call A’s home games. Callahan was hired by the Golden State Warriors way back in 1981 and was their announcer for 19 years. For an additional 12 years, from 2000 until 2012, he became the voice of the Cal Golden Bears football team. He also worked various St. Mary’s College basketball games where he began his announcing career in 1975.
articles.title: Dick Callahan, former announcer for A’s, Warriors, & Cal, dies

articles.text: The annual Firefall routinely attracts hundreds of professional photographers to Horsetail Falls in Yosemite. Expected viewing this year falls between Feb. 11-27 with the best anticipated day to be on Feb. 21 from 5:28 p.m. to 5:40 p.m. Mother nature always calls the shots with this event, which requires a clear sky. “This unique lighting effect happens only on evenings with a clear sky when the waterfall is flowing. Even some haze or minor cloudiness can greatly diminish or eliminate the effect,” wrote park officials. Park officials are directing visitors to park at the Yosemite Falls and Yosemite Lodge Parking lot, and walk 1.5 miles to near the El Capitan Picnic Area for the best view of the Firefall. Visitors would be wise to arrive hours early to camp out for a prime viewing location, preparing for cold weather and a headlamp for the return walk in the dark. Northside Drive will have one lane closed to vehicles so pedestrians can walk on the road between the viewing area and Yosemite Falls parking. Photo courtesy of Travel & Leisure
articles.title: Firefall viewing information
