pages.text: Wednesday, February 3, 2021 15 HIKING WITH JON A winter surprise: Uvas Canyon’s waterfalls roaring after rains By Jonathan Comeaux Our weekend adventure moved us out of the Bay Area to Morgan Hill, the location of a 1,147-acre park known for its series of waterfalls. Located on the eastern side of the Santa Cruz Mountains is Uvas Canyon County Park, found at the very end of the private Sveadal community on Croy Road. The recent rains that drenched the Bay Area helped awaken waterfalls along Swanson and Alec Creek. Hikers are greeted by the sound of babbling brooks immediately when entering the park on the Waterfall Loop trail along Swanson Creek. The first and smallest cascade, Granuja Falls, provides a fitting welcome to visitors after the first bridge. After another half mile, hikers will find the base of the Black Rock Falls on the right. Follow the water up the narrow path to a roughly 20-foot waterfall that passes over a black rock face, hence its name. Returning back to the Waterfall Loop Trail for just 0.2 of a Black Rock Falls is around 20 feet tall and feeds into Swanson Creek. Upper Falls is about 15 feet tall and is situated close to Basin Falls. Triple Falls is the final of five thriving waterfalls in the park. It’s the tallest at around 50 feet. Staff Photos Uvas Canyon County Park in Morgan Hill has a collection of waterfalls that are easily accessible for hikers. Pictured here is Basin Falls. The first of the falls is the smallest, Garunja Falls. mile brings walkers to an intersection with the base of Upper Falls on the left, and a walkway to Basin Falls, which seemed to be the most thriving in the park after the rain. Basin Falls is about 15 feet in height, flowing down stones as it feeds into Swanson Creek. A fallen tree sits in its center to provide a clear perspective of its size. Returning to the Waterfall loop reunites you with Upper Falls, a two-tiered cascade that is also around 15 feet tall. Passing the falls means you are nearing the halfway point of your hike as you venture onto the Contour Trail. The Contour Trail goes for about 1.1 miles and provides some uphill climb, meaning it’s not just a scenic nature hike, but a fitting lower body workout. The trail is enveloped with the aroma of California Bay Laurels, the sprawling red bark of Manzanita, and some towering second-growth redwoods. After intersecting with the Alec Canyon Trail, turn right and hike less than a mile to Triple Falls – the final landmark of the day. It is the tallest of the falls, roughly 50 feet tall, but is really a small trickle compared to the other four. To see every waterfall on the Uvas Canyon loop is a hike of approximately 5.2 miles. It tops out at 1,273 feet in elevation gain. We passed 44 hikers on the day, but 36 were on the initial walk, the popular Waterfall Loop trail. Uvas Canyon is one of the few dog-friendly parks in the Santa Cruz Mountains, so it is safe to bring your pooch. Advance reservations are needed for parking – 24 hours in advance - otherwise you’ll be parking on the road leading in. Punch in “Uvas Canyon County Park” to your GPS device to access this South Bay park. A view of the active Swanson Creek. Hikers cross over the creek to continue on the Contour Trail. The Contour Trail is narrow and envelops hikers in the lush greenery of the Santa Cruz Mountains.

articles.text: “Entwined” by Charles Gadeken. The public art installation is located adjacent to the Conservatory of Flowers in Golden Gate Park. Visitors are now flocking to Peacock Meadow in Golden Gate Park to see its transformation into an enchanted forest of otherworldly shapes and ever-changing light. “Entwined,” a public art installation by San Francisco artist Charles Gadeken, creates a whimsical wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees while practicing social distancing. San Francisco is under a stayat-home order, but the parks are still open to the public. “Entwined” is available to view from dusk until 8:30 p.m., but the lawn portion of the meadow remains closed due to muddy conditions. Everyone must wear a mask at all times and practice social distancing. City and County of San Francisco’s current health order suggests that guests visit with household members only. Viewing is free and tickets are not required.
articles.title: Public Art now on display in Golden Gate Park

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will present its second digital program of the season on February 11. Dwight Rhoden’s “Let’s Begin at the End” returns digitally, following its success at the 2018 Unbound Festival. Composers include Bach, Philip Glass, and Michael Nyman. The program continues with San Francisco Ballet soloist Myles Thatcher, known for his signature blend of movement and social consciousness, who will showcase a new work in a world premiere. The program concludes with an archival capture of “Sandpaper Ballet,” a clever tongue-incheek piece from choreographer Mark Morris. Streaming access is available beginning 6 p.m. on February 11, and single stream access is available. Behind-the-scenes resources can be found on San Francisco Ballet’s website. Visit https://www.sf ballet.org/productions/digital-program-02/ to obtain tickets to these digital events.
articles.title: SF Ballet to present “Let’s Begin at the End” on February 11

articles.text: San Francisco Opera’s Department of Diversity will present “For the Love of Opera,” a series of conversations during February about experiences of love on the lyric stage. It will follow with a Women’s History Month celebration throughout March. The first panel will explore LGBTQ+ storylines in 21st century opera. The speaker series begins with countertenor Albert Montanez, who has performed internationally and was chosen for the title role in the world premiere of the Alan Turing Opera Project in Sweden. He obtained an Artist Diploma at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London and received a full scholarship from the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. The artist discussion will begin on Sunday, February 7 at 7 p.m. Each 75-minute Zoom discussion is part of Opera Aficionado, a weekly interactive lecture series that offers music lovers around the world a front-row seat to scholarly talks, panels and conversations and an opportunity to dialogue with fellow opera enthusiasts, composers and special guests. Each virtual lecture is $20 and holds a maximum capacity of 20 attendees. A limited number of discounted tickets are available upon request for individuals in Albert Montanez need. Tickets are available until noon on the day of each event. Visit https://www.sfarts.org/ event/lgbtq-love-in-21stcentury-albert-montaez-37eR2lIdStMby5ZM96gTBG to obtain tickets. 510-525-5656 Monday-Friday 8:30-5:30 Saturday 9:00-5:00 Sunday Closed CARPET | VINYL | WOOD | LINOLEUM BETWEEN GILMAN & BUCHANAN ST. articles.text: Cristiana Pegoraro, a world-renowned pianist who has performed in Piedmont, released a new music video on January 27 to commemorate International Holocaust Day. Pegoraro, from Narni, Italy, is Artistic Director of the celebrated Narnia Festival. She is considered one of the most gifted pianists and composers of her generation. In 2006 and 2007, she toured the Gulf countries, becoming the first Italian female pianist to perform classical concerts in Bahrain, Yemen, and Oman. She is also the first female pianist to perform the 32 Sonatas for piano by Ludwig van Beethoven. In 2018 Piedmont Center for the Arts (PCA) welcomed her for an inspired concert, fresh from her popular appearance at Carnegie Hall in New York. Her performance at the Center was through her personal and professional friendship with PCA board member Debbie Dare and her husband Joseph Gold. articles.text: The Piedmont-based band, The Whiskey Talking, has been performing throughout the Bay Area for the last 15 years. But it wasn’t until last week, January 22, that the band finally released its debut album, “Grounded,” which is now available on all streaming services, CD and vinyl. The album contains 10 original songs written and sung by Piedmont resident Scott Lawson. It features Piedmont resident Paul Kasrovi on bass, as well as Terry Wit on drums. The music is a blend of rock, country, and folk, an amalgam typically referred to as “Americana.” The album comes out of the chute with a bang with a driving, punkish number called “Staggers and Jags.” “’Staggers and Jags’ is a British expression referring to delirium tremens,” explained Lawson. “The song is loosely about a couple I knew in L.A. who, like so many people down there, were constantly torn between their desire for spiritual awakening and their inherent decadence – the kind of people who would pause a meditation session to do a line.” The ballad “Red River” is a true story about the girlfriend of a former band member. “The two of them were living in New Mexico at the time. Apparently, they had a fight and she drove off into the Sangre de Cristo mountains above Taos,” said Lawson. “She was found the following day in her car, near the town of Red River, frozen to death. The car still had a half tank of gas and was working fine. Why she died is a complete mystery.” Jacket cover of CD issued by The Whiskey Talking, Scott Lawson’s Piedmont-based band. The song’s chorus asks: “Did you leave on your own terms? And were all of your lessons learned? Did you think it was better to freeze than to burn?” Over its 42 minutes, the album covers a lot of musical and lyrical ground, from the Southern-rock inflected road song, “Angel of Mercy,” to a country ballad, “Everybody Seems to Wanna Know,” to the anti-war rock of “Food Chain,” and the pastoral float of “Flying Dream.” Kasrovi said that the band members each come from different musical perspectives and those are reflected in the diversity of the genres they explore. In “previous lives,” all three band members played in modestly successful bands in Los Angeles and New York. “Scott and I both regularly played places like The Roxy and The Troubadour and The House of Blues back in the 80s and 90s, and Terry used to play at CBGB’s in New York,” Kasrovi said. “But what we have with this band is different – and better.” The album, released on Hardscrabble Records, can be heard by visiting http://thewhiskeytalking.hearnow.com or simply by searching for The Whiskey Talking on Spotify or other streaming services.
articles.title: CD 15 years in the making by Scott Lawson’s band, The Whiskey Talking

articles.text: The Fong Costanza Trio joins Ben Simon for a special extended episode of “Simon Says Show.” While the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra ensemble shelters in place, Music Director Ben Simon has put his time in quarantine to good use by launching the “Simon Says Show.” Simon has added new episodes and his series continues with a performance by the Fong Costanza Trio. The San Francisco Chamber Orchestra’s principal second violinist, Debra Fong, is joined by spouse Chris Costanza and daughter Isabella Costanza for a special family project. The trio came together via Zoom to perform on Simon’s series recently. The performance is featured in a special “extended episode” with a runtime of 52 minutes. Watch and listen to the trio at https://www.thesfco.org/simonsaysshow.
articles.title: ‘Simon Says’ show continues with Fong Costanza Trio

articles.text: The ensembla cast of Rian Johnson’s Knives Out. Movie review by Chris Honoré Mysteries represent a massive literary genre so compelling that it has found a solid niche on television and in film. A captivating example is the just released Knives Out, written and directed by Rian Johnson in which he pays homage to those writers and filmmakers who came before, unabashedly using their familiar templates. The story is set in New England, primarily in a century-old Gothic mansion. A large extended family (Jamie Lee Curtis, Michael Shannon, Don Johnson, Toni Colette and Chris Evans) has gathered to celebrate the 85th birthday of Harlan Thrombey (Christopher Plummer), a wildly successful and prolific mystery writer who has amassed a fortune from the sale of his books. Harlan sits at the titular head of the table as the unchallenged patriarch of a cohort of grown children and grandchildren, plus a young nurse, Marta (Ana de Armas). To a person (with the exception of Marta) they seem ever mindful of the inheritance dangling before them like a modifier, consuming the subtext of their interactions. Later in the evening, Harlan is discovered in his third-floor attic study by Marta, who was bringing him a meal. His throat has been cut. Terrified, she runs downstairs to the family who are gathered in a sitting room. And thus, the narrative abruptly shifts to a what/why/whodunit, giving structure to all that follows. Arriving with the police is a private detective, Benoit Blanc (Daniel Craig), who is initially content to sit in the shadows, listening. Finally, when asked, he acknowledges that he was hired by an anonymous individual and will be assisting, without police objection, in the investigation. He asks that each family member be interviewed, suggesting that they should remain at the house. They agree, anticipating a funeral service for Harlan, followed by a reading of the will. Soon Blanc morphs into the puzzle master, questioning each of them in his Col. Sanders drawl, collecting vagrant bits of information, all while assuming they are reflexively dissembling. Slowly, tenaciously, the onion is peeled in the search of motive and opportunity. Loose ends are ubiquitous and in need of being tied up. Some are quickly discarded for more likely outcomes. Suspects are everywhere (of course it could have been a suicide… or not). Detective Blanc grows increasingly more animated as he assembles the puzzle, beginning with the borders and working toward the center, waiting for an image, however obscured, to emerge. Screenwriter Johnson clearly takes genuine pleasure in the genre, the plot replete with twists and head fakes and delicious reveals. Those in the audience have to pay attention or miss what is offered up as a clue: a broken trellis, a silent dowager, footprints on a muddy path, an overheard argument, a missing medicine bag, a volatile grandson. And then there’s young, devoted Marta, the full-time nurse – an immigrant of sorts (sneeringly accused of being an anchor baby) – who is slowly pulled into the center of the Thrombey clan’s many residual issues. These are people who have more baggage than a hotel lobby and are ever prepared to pull out the knives honed by familial history and have a go at one another. I’m reluctant to say more about the plot; the pleasure derived from watching Knives Out is seeing it fresh, in effect, clueless. Thankfully, the trailer was sufficiently ambiguous, giving only a hint of what the film promised. Even Harlan speaks from the grave as the mystery inextricably unfolds. And so it does – in the attic study, with a knife, and not a candlestick anywhere to be found. Knives Out (2019). Directed by Rian Johnson. With Jamie Lee Curtis, Michael Shannon, Don Johnson, Christopher Plummer, Toni Colette and Chris Evans. 2 hrs., 10 min. PG-13. articles.text: Octavia Spencer and Viola Davis stars in The Help. There is so much to like in The Help, so many reasons to recommend. And yet there is also a sense that there is something missing. Perhaps that’s because it is set in the South, during the nascent days of the Civil Rights movement, when Jim Crow laws and attitudes The film, written and directed by Tate Taylor, adapted from Kathryn Stockett’s bestseller, is from the point of view of countless black women who, in the early 1960s still worked as maids in the homes of the wealthy white families of Jackson, Mississippi. The narrative voice is Skeeter’s (Emma Stone), newly returned to Jackson from Ole Miss. She lands a job working for the local newspaper and is inspired to interview the maids of those Junior League women who lead privileged, insulated lives and are trapped by their own These daughters of the South are incapable of seeing their maids as three-dimensional people; rather, they view them as accessories, and thus avoid real engagement with their children or with the hard labor that is required to run their homes. It is the maids who cook the meals, buy their groceries, clean their houses and raise Skeeter begins by interviewing two maids – Abileen (Viola Davis) and Minny (Octavia Spencer) – probing their lives and drawing out their stories and their feelings about the white children they have nurtured. Abileen has cared for 17 children during her decades of service. Each morning, dressed in uniforms, these women leave their shotgun bungalows and take the bus to the homes of the white families. It is there that the morality play, which is at the heart of The Help, is played out. And it is there that Abileen and Minny suffer in silence, ever fearful of a misstep, as the bigoted young women display, without reflection, a racism laced with a condescending, brittle intolerance. What the film doesn’t accomplish – and perhaps it’s unfair to expect that it could – is to graphically explore the depth of the injustice and anger hidden just beneath the patina of civility. The Help is wonderfully acted, led by Viola Davis and Octavia Spencer, whose astonishing performances – which never slip into caricature – are nicely supported by Emma Stone, Allison Janney, and Bryce Dallas Howard in a tour de force of villainy. The film is predicated on the archetype of African American women – maternal, non-threatening, ever-smiling, middle aged – who, from the early days of slavery, were central to the plantation manor. The Help. Directed by Tate Taylor. Starring Emma Stone, Viola Davis and Octavia Spencer. 2 hrs., 17 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: The Help a look at Jackson, Miss. in the sixties

articles.text: Ivan Vanko, portrayed by Mickey Rourke, is Tony Stark’s nemesis in Iron Man 2. Movie review by Chris Honoré The first Iron Man movie was released in 2008. It had a high “wow factor” to be sure. It was fresh and interesting, a shiny adaptation of the Marvel Comics’ character, Iron Man, brought to life by the talented actor Robert Downey. Iron Man 1 delivered the necessary backstory regarding how Iron Man came to be, along with the astonishing technology that turned Tony Stark, industrialist, into a high-flying weapons system. The Iron Man suit defines cool. Plus, it’s always a thrill watching a superhero’s history unfold, watching as he or she begins to take control of newly discovered and unexpected abilities. Recall Superman, arriving on earth in the center of a meteor; or Spider Man, bitten by a spider, grappling with his metamorphosis. It’s a rush. Hence, that first Iron Man movie, now in franchise mode, was superb entertainment. The challenge then was how to craft a sequel that would be equally gripping. Comic book adaptations have become an entertainment staple using familiar characters: Batman, Hulk, X-Men, Superman, Spider Man, and Hellboy, to name a few. Which brings us to Iron Man 2. For writer Justin Theroux and director Don Favreau the trick was to find a story that presented a now established Tony Stark aka Iron Man in a new and interesting way. A new antagonist had to be introduced, an opponent worthy of Stark’s incomparable strength, wealth and intelligence. If not done well the filmmakers risked “jumping the shark,” meaning that the Iron Man 1 narrative had peaked with the first film and anything thereafter would be anti-climactic. The term “jump the shark” is most often used to describe the moment when a TV series or movie franchise begins its downturn and things spin off into absurdity. If “jump the shark” doesn’t do justice to the phenomenon, there’s always “Nuke the fridge,” derived from the moment in Indiana Jones and the Crystal Skull, the second in the trilogy, when Indy jumps into a lead-lined fridge and survives a nuclear explosion unscathed. The scene was so far from the inimitable first film, Indiana Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Ark, that it acquired its own moniker, “Nuke the fridge.” So, does Iron Man 2 “nuke the fridge”? Pretty much. In an effort to make Stark extraordinary and more complex, the writers make him decidedly un-heroic. He’s arrogant, hubristic, and seemingly consumed with his newfound fame and power. Basically, he’s not very appealing. In one scene he arrives before a government oversight committee with studied insouciance, flashing the peace sign, declaring world peace has been privatized, while displaying an ego that is in need of deflating. Watching Robert Downey portray even a phone book is always a treat. But this second incarnation of Stark is simply strange. Downey is, of course, a consummate actor as is Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts, his unacknowledged love interest and solidly competent girl Friday. As for Mickey Rourke, in all his grungy splendor, well, he’s passable as a Russian named Ivan Vanko, wingnut scientist, and Stark’s bad dude nemesis. Samuel L. Jackson makes an appearance, briefly, as Nick Fury as does Scarlett Johansson in the role of Natalie, aka Black Widow. The burden that any sequel carries is one of story. Once Iron Man’s history has been revealed, and his superhero talents established, it all comes down to imagination. Does Iron Man 2 have the right stuff? Sadly, the answer is no. The hardware is wonderful. The suit is still a treat to watch: wax on, wax off. But the rest, the loud climactic battle, the flights at supersonic speeds – all of it is familiar. The fallback position should be craft a great screenplay. Otherwise, the thrill is gone. Iron Man 2. Starring Robert Downey, Don Cheadle, Gwyneth Paltrow, Scarlett Johansson and Mickey Rourke. Directed by Jon Favreau. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Iron Man 2 lacks excitement of first

articles.text: A scene from The Secret of NIMH. Movie review by Chris Honoré The Secret of NIMH is a wonderful, compelling story, both whimsical and thrilling. Its handdrawn animation is extraordinary, rich in detail and color, and follows in that familiar tradition in which animals talk and reason. It was adapted from the 1971 children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, written by Robert C. O’Brien. From the opening scene, the narrative is flooded with a sense of urgency that fully engages the audience. Mrs. Frisby (Elizabeth Harman), a widowed mouse, lives with her two children in a cinder block located in an open field on the Fitzgibbon farm. She learns that the field is soon to be plowed and she must move her family as quickly as possible to a safe place. But she is confronted with what seems an insurmountable problem: she discovers that her child Timothy is ill. She asks Mr. Ages (Arthur Mallet), a friend of her late husband, Jonathan, to come see her young son. He tells Mrs. Frisby that Timothy is very sick with pneumonia, gives her some medicine, and adds that Timothy cannot be moved for at least three weeks. The following day she learns that Farmer Fitzgibbons is going to start plowing early. Suddenly, time is of the essence, and she realizes that she needs help. With her friend Jeremy (Dom DeLuise), a clumsy but comical crow, she goes to consult the Great Owl (John Carradine) for advice. pages.text: Wednesday, February 3, 2021 19 MOVIES FOR KIDS Iron Man 2 lacks excitement of first Ivan Vanko, portrayed by Mickey Rourke, is Tony Stark’s nemesis in Iron Man 2. Movie review by Chris Honoré The first Iron Man movie was released in 2008. It had a high “wow factor” to be sure. It was fresh and interesting, a shiny adaptation of the Marvel Comics’ character, Iron Man, brought to life by the talented actor Robert Downey. Iron Man 1 delivered the necessary backstory regarding how Iron Man came to be, along with the astonishing technology that turned Tony Stark, industrialist, into a high-flying weapons system. The Iron Man suit defines cool. Plus, it’s always a thrill watching a superhero’s history unfold, watching as he or she begins to take control of newly discovered and unexpected abilities. Recall Superman, arriving on earth in the center of a meteor; or Spider Man, bitten by a spider, grappling with his metamorphosis. It’s a rush. Hence, that first Iron Man movie, now in franchise mode, was superb entertainment. The challenge then was how to craft a sequel that would be equally gripping. Comic book adaptations have become an entertainment staple using familiar characters: Batman, Hulk, X-Men, Superman, Spider Man, and Hellboy, to name a few. Which brings us to Iron Man 2. For writer Justin Theroux and director Don Favreau the trick was to find a story that presented a now established Tony Stark aka Iron Man in a new and interesting way. A new antagonist had to be introduced, an opponent worthy of Stark’s incomparable strength, wealth and intelligence. If not done well the filmmakers risked “jumping the shark,” meaning that the Iron Man 1 narrative had peaked with the first film and anything thereafter would be anti-climactic. The term “jump the shark” is most often used to describe the moment when a TV series or movie franchise begins its downturn and things spin off into absurdity. If “jump the shark” doesn’t do justice to the phenomenon, there’s always “Nuke the fridge,” derived from the moment in Indiana Jones and the Crystal Skull, the second in the trilogy, when Indy jumps into a lead-lined fridge and survives a nuclear explosion unscathed. The scene was so far from the inimitable first film, Indiana Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Ark, that it acquired its own moniker, “Nuke the fridge.” So, does Iron Man 2 “nuke the fridge”? Pretty much. In an effort to make Stark extraordinary and more complex, the writers make him decidedly un-heroic. He’s arrogant, hubristic, and seemingly consumed with his newfound fame and power. Basically, he’s not very appealing. In one scene he arrives before a government oversight committee with studied insouciance, flashing the peace sign, declaring world peace has been privatized, while displaying an ego that is in need of deflating. Watching Robert Downey portray even a phone book is always a treat. But this second incarnation of Stark is simply strange. Downey is, of course, a consummate actor as is Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts, his unacknowledged love interest and solidly competent girl Friday. As for Mickey Rourke, in all his grungy splendor, well, he’s passable as a Russian named Ivan Vanko, wingnut scientist, and Stark’s bad dude nemesis. Samuel L. Jackson makes an appearance, briefly, as Nick Fury as does Scarlett Johansson in the role of Natalie, aka Black Widow. The burden that any sequel carries is one of story. Once Iron Man’s history has been revealed, and his superhero talents established, it all comes down to imagination. Does Iron Man 2 have the right stuff? Sadly, the answer is no. The hardware is wonderful. The suit is still a treat to watch: wax on, wax off. But the rest, the loud climactic battle, the flights at supersonic speeds – all of it is familiar. The fallback position should be craft a great screenplay. Otherwise, the thrill is gone. Iron Man 2. Starring Robert Downey, Don Cheadle, Gwyneth Paltrow, Scarlett Johansson and Mickey Rourke. articles.text: Evelyn and her Magic Violin. Evelyn Kaye, a Julliard-trained violinist, was a beautiful violinist in addition to having movie star looks. She was well-known as a featured performer with Phil Spitalny’s Hour of Charm Orchestra. Everyone needs a wake-up call once in a while. I got mine at the beginning of the year. I wanted to interview my favorite opera singer, so I went through the usual channels and contacted his manager. There was no response after three attempts. I tried once more and the manager responded. I would get no interview. The manager said that: “Larry is busy and has too many things to do.“ Some guys have all the luck. Wake-up calls like this are quite useful. They cause us to think about some pretty serious stuff… like rejection. This caused me to think about why some performers have it all and others who are equally talented languish. The history of music is illustrated by a struggle for supremacy. In politics, success is usually on the side of the biggest army. Music is not so far removed. As a case in point, King David must have had a good publicity department. So did Nero, who embraced the ageold adage that bad publicity is the same as good publicity – as long as they spell your name correctly. Politics has lobbyists; music has payola. But putting politics aside, how can we, the music loving public, discover our heroes? Are today’s icons really the best, or are the power brokers lurking in the shadows? Don King, the famed boxing promoter, is not unique in history. Long before social media took over, to be successful and be recognized, an aspiring artist had to petition the local nobleman. Only then was permission granted. The church played a similar role. Then, as now, many would sell their souls to the devil for fame and fortune. Enter Niccolò Paganini; perhaps the greatest violinist of all time. Perhaps. But there is no doubt that he was the greatest exploiter of publicity ever. Every successful performer has studied how Paganini did it – even Sinatra and Elvis and the Beatles. Everyone. Competitions are one way to stardom. Almost every first-prize winner at the Paris Conservatory enjoyed a successful career. Some notable names are Wieniawski, Sarasate, and Fritz Kreisler. In composition it was Berlioz and Bizet. They were great and unique talents. Today competitions are commonplace. Contestants go from one to the other, and in doing so stunt their growth artistically. Some performers are pure media creations. Mario Lanza is the best example. His public concerts were so rare that you can count them on your fingers. But he was a great singer, Hollywood and television not withstanding. Frank Sinatra was ever so popular. His mafia connections delivered – big time. Corporations sometimes help. I know, for a fact, that a big Japanese firm paid $4.5 million for a violin and gifted it to a notable player. In the world of race car driving, if you want to win the Grand Prix, it helps to have a Ferrari. It is always fun to be a Monday morning quarterback. Initiate the debate and then stand back. Watch from the bleachers, but never go onto the field. Sometimes the scene is funny. Remember the “merchandising“ scene from Spaceballs? George Foreman took it to heart and mastered it. But so did famed operetta composer Franz Lehar. He was pictured in a magazine ad. He had shaving cream on his face and a razor in his hand. The caption: “I get my greatest musical inspirations using brand X shaving cream.“ To prove my point, look at the visuals. Even Jascha Heifetz did it. Another example is a Maybelline ad with Evelyn and her magic violin. Some artists have all the luck. They are all things to all people – talented, savvy, well connected… and good looking. The common business model for all of them was they didn’t turn down interviews.

articles.text: Online exhibitions continue throughout the month of February The University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley. The University of California Botanical Garden in Berkeley is open to the public during COVID-19 restrictions, but reservations are required to visit. The gardens are open daily from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Members-only hours are from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. The gardens are closed on the first Tuesday of the month. The glasshouses, water fountains and garden shop are temporarily closed due to COVID, and will reopen when Alameda County enters a less-restrictive tier of COVID-19 regulations. Guests should note that there will be path disruptions throughout the garden as staff works to manage visitation flow and allow for important horticultural projects. Restrooms, benches, and water bottle filling stations are available. Online advanced admission tickets are required for all visitors, including members. Reservations must be made online via a timed-ticketing reservation system before you arrive at the garden. To reserve tickets, click on https://botanicalgarden.berkeley. edu/covid-reopen. To experience the gardens from home, take advantage of the online exhibits. Throughout February, UC Botanical Garden will present its annual exhibition and celebration of botanical art on a digital platform. Visit the Garden’s website throughout the month of February to view a stunning array of art featuring plants from around the world. You can also join garden staff for an opening “reception” on Zoom on Saturday February 6 from 5 p.m. to 6 p.m. There are also associated Zoom programs, such as a lecture on the history of botanical art on February 12, an introduction to botanical art on February 20, and a 3-part series titled “Inside the Artists’ Studio”, which will take you on a visit to the studios of six artists demonstrating techniques in botanical art. To view more online resources, see https://events.berkeley.edu/ index.php/calendar/sn/bot.html?eve nt _ I D =136805&d at e = 2021-02-06&filter=Event%20 Type&filtersel=.
articles.title: UC Botanical Garden is open; reservations required

articles.text: A group of artistic and entrepreneurial Piedmont and Oakland residents will gather this Saturday, February 6 on the sidewalk surrounding a Crocker Highlands home to sell their arts, crafts, homemade food products and more. With Valentine’s Day just around the corner, many of the items will be specifically designed as gifts for the February 14 holiday. The sale begins at 11 a.m. and goes until 3 p.m. The location of the sale is 855 Longridge Road at the corner of Verrada. It is approximately two blocks up from Lakeshore. Artist and former Piedmonter Lisa Scimens will be selling her original Valentine cards, coffee mugs and pillows. Also for sale will be samples from her Dancing Artist Designs online store (www.dancingartistdesigns.com) and other greeting cards featuring artwork from her paintings. All sales will benefit Family Sanity, her non-profit organization that helps parents with young adults and teens challenged by mental illness (www.familysanity.org). articles.text: Celebrate the Year of the Ox with Asian Art Museum. San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum will offer an array of digital events to celebrate Lunar New Year, the Year of the Ox. Lunar New Year is the beginning of a calendar year whose months are cycles of the moon. It is widely celebrated in East Asia and Southeast Asia, as well as other parts of the world. You can learn more about how Lunar New Year is observed around the world with the museum’s cultural celebration packet. Visit https:// asianart.org/cultural-celebrations/celebrate-lunar-new-year/ to view on-line resources. Included in the celebration packets are art activities, coloring pages, and a Lunar New Year Red Envelope instructional project. A storyteller series features Fred Sheng, Miriam Mills, and Leta Bushyhead reading classic celebratory tales. A New Year poetry and calligraphy workshop will take place tomorrow, February 4, at 7 p.m. Poets Michael Warr and Chun Yu will read works in English and Mandarin that reflect the essence of the New Year – vanquishing the past, embracing new beginnings, and venerating ancestors – while Aiqin Zhou demonstrates her skillful calligraphy by illustrating some of the poems. The Ox is the second of the 12-year periodic sequence of animals, which appear in the Chinese zodiac. The Year of the Ox follows after the Year of the Rat (2020), and is followed by the Year of the Tiger (2022). To learn more about the symbolic significance of the Ox, visit https://asianart.org/.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Mmmm, good. Chocolate Cherry Scones will put a smile on everyone’s face in time for Valentine’s Day. Scones in winter are an easy, one-bowl creation with basic ingredients many of us have on hand – flour, butter, cream, and sugar. In winter I prefer to make them by hand, using my fingers to massage the cold bits of butter into the flour mixture. It’s fast and somehow satisfying, and it’s an easier clean-up than bringing in a food processor or even a pastry cutter. I figure I’m going to need to get in there with my fingers to pat, shape and cut the scones anyway, so why not go fully manual? This version is fancy, but still using common pantry ingredients, chocolate and dried cherries. Feel free to substitute dried cranberries, snipped dried apricots, even candied citrus or ginger bits. Chocolate Cherry Cream Scones Adapted from Clair Ptak’s Cream Scones and David Burtka’s Chocolate & Cherry Scones. Makes 12 scones, about 3” diameter INGREDIENTS • • • • • • • • • • • • • 2-1/2 cups all-purpose flour, plus more for shaping 1/4 cup granulated sugar 1 tablespoon baking powder 1/2 teaspoon baking soda 1/8 teaspoon salt 1/2 cup unsalted butter, chilled and cut into 1/4-inch cubes 1/2 cup dried cherries, soft and pliable 1/2 cup dark chocolate pieces, either chopped from a bar or chocolate chips 3/4 cups heavy cream, chilled 1/2 cup buttermilk, chilled 1 teaspoon vanilla extract 1 egg, beaten Turbinado sugar, or other coarse sugar to top DIRECTIONS 0 Line a baking sheet with parchment paper. 1 Combine together the flour, baking powder, baking soda and salt; then stir in the sugar in a large mixing bowl, at least 3-quart size. Make sure all the dry ingredients are thoroughly mixed. Set aside. 2 Cut the butter into 1/ 2” cubes and rub through the dry ingredients with your fingers, a pastry cutter, or use a food processor—anyway that results in a coarse, crumbly texture. 3 Add the vanilla extract into the heavy cream, then pour the cream and buttermilk over the top of the flour mixture; gently stir with a wooden spoon until just combined. Add the chopped chocolate and dried cherries and stir to just distribute evenly throughout. 4 Turn the mixture onto a lightly floured surface and press together into a block. 5 Fold the dough in half, lifting and turning the dough over itself just once. Press together and let it rest for 5 minutes. 6 Pat the dough into about a 1” thick round. Use a 2-1/ 2” round cutter to stamp out the scones, pressing straight down through the dough and straight back out. Do not twist the cutter, as it hinders the scones’ rise. Gently reshape the dough back to a 1” thickness as needed to total 12 scones. Take care to not handle the dough too much. 7 Transfer the scones onto the lined baking sheet. Cover with plastic wrap and place in the fridge or freezer for 10 to 20 minutes to rest. This helps the scones keep their shape while baking. 8 Meanwhile, adjust a rack to the lower third position in the oven and preheat the oven to 400° F. 9 When ready, remove the scones from their chilly rest and brush each with the egg wash and sprinkle lightly with the turbinado sugar. Bake for about 20-25 minutes until golden. 10 Remove from the oven and transfer to a wire rack to cool. HAPPY VALENTINE’S DAY! For more information or to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok at PiedmontPantry.com.

pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 3, 2021 Features your Oakland Zoo welcomes everyone back By Jay Russell Oakland Zoo reopened to the public today, February 3, after being closed for 58 days since the Shelter-in-Place went into effect December 7. And in some equally good news, Glowfari, the Zoo’s nighttime glowing lantern extravaganza, will reopen on Friday, February 5. “We’re excited to be able to reopen the Zoo and welcome back our guests,” said Joel Parrott, President & CEO of the Oakland Zoo. “During this second closure, our focus has been to go above and beyond to protect the health and safety of every guest, staff member and animal,” he added. Dr. Parrott recently announced that after 37 years with the Zoo he While the Oakland Zoo was closed, some new friends took up residence. Nonami, a Schmidt’s red-tailed monkey native to the forests of Africa’s Congo, is now available for visitors to see. Here to Help with Temporary Respite Care will be retiring later this Spring. The Zoo was more prepared to close this time, after the first closure of 132 days at the start of the pandemic. “We received a tremendous amount of support financially through donations during our first closure that was useful during our second (shorter) closure. That being said, guest admission is our primary source of revenue, and we are grateful this closure is ending sooner than the last,” said Isabella Linares, the Zoo’s Marketing Associate. Daily Zoo hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The zoo still is using a timed ticketing reservation system that requires advance online purchase for specific dates and arrival time. Big crowds are no more. The maximum capacity has been reduced to 2,900, down from a maximum of 7,000 visitors during peak normal times. Glowfari, the exciting, illuminated lantern festival, will resume as well, with tickets going on sale starting this Friday at 10 a.m. The nighttime event that took the place of Zoo Lights features something for everyone, with larger-than-life-size animal lanterns and realistic animatronic dinosaurs. Due to popular demand, Glowfari has been extended until March 13, running seven days a week from 5:30 p.m. to 10:00 p.m. The zoo has kept busy during this most recent closure. Zoo staff were able to undertake major landscaping projects to update the horticulture for guests and animals. Look who’s new at the zoo Some new friends have moved in recently, including M’Zuzi, a male Hamadryas baboon born in the zoo on December 29. More primate pals joined in the party during the closure with the addition of Schmidt’s red-tailed monkeys who now inhabit the African Savanna exhibit at the Zoo. Zoo guests will enjoy seeing their animal friends. The macaws, chimpanzees, giraffes and squirrel monkeys love interacting with guests and have needed extra attention from staff while visitors have been absent. To reserve tickets, go to oaklandzoo.org or call (510) 632-9525. Oakland Zoo is located at 9777 Golf Links Road in Oakland. articles.text: Jill Biden with the presidential dogs, Major and Champ. Dear Abby: Can you tell us anything about the First Dogs that now reside in the White House? I’m curious! –Tina and Dill the Frenchie Dear Tina and Dill: There are two male German Shepherds, named Major and Champ, now living in the White House. Major is about two years old, and is the first rescue dog to live in the White House. He loves running on the South Lawn while the 12-year-old Champ enjoys sleeping in the new dog bed by the fireplace. There are rumors that Major may help raise awareness and money for shelters. According to the First Lady, Jill Biden, a cat will soon be joining them. The last cat to live in the White House was Willie, a member of the George W. Bush family, and before that was Socks, the famous cat of Pres. Clinton. The White House was not completely finished when the first “First Dogs” moved in and began patrolling in the 1800’s. Bow wow, meow, –Abby Dear Abby: Is there any way dogs can help in the Pandemic? What can we do? –Ben and Olivia the Springer Spaniel Dear Ben and Olivia: I think the best you can do is to help each other to stay sane and safe until you get a vaccine. Apparently cuddling with a pet can lower blood pressure and diminish stress. Taking a walk or a hike (with a mask) is always helpful for general good health, so make a point to sneak out between rain showers and breathe. A dog in Turkey named Boncuk (beads) made a point of visiting the hospital her owner was taken to. Apparently, she would just wait by the hospital door from 9 a.m. until nightfall before returning home for dinner. A few times the owner’s family tried to bring her home early, but she would just return to the doors of the hospital. True loyalty. When the owner was finally released, Boncuk was wagging her tail and happily walking by the wheelchair as the owner hugged her. That’s a loyal dog. Tail wags to Boncuk, –Abby Dear Abby: I’d like to get my mom and dad a present for Valentine’s Day. Any ideas of what I can give them without going to a store? I’m not a good shopper but I’d like to say thanks. –Goose the rescued Mix Dear Goose: Bay Area artist Judy North can paint your mug for your folks so they will always have you on canvas and in their hearts. She’ll start by spending some time with you and snapping two to three rolls of film before painting you. Judy is a dog lover, and her goal is to capture your true spirit. Her work was shown on the walls of the Slanted Door restaurant in San Francisco for years. Check out her website at Judynorth.com. Or ask a family member to capture you in a drawing and then immortalize it on a cotton tote. Your folks will not only have a doggone image of you, but a piece of the family’s artwork, too. Cotton Tote Bag by Cece DuPraz comes with instructions, special paper, colored pencils and a ruler. The drawing you pick is then sent off and embroidered on the tote to have for a long, long time. Go to Neimanmarcus.com for more information. Lastly, there’s a magical book called The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse by Charlie Mackesy that not only inspires one to love animals but each other, no matter what shape or size or smell. Can’t wait to hear about which K9 surprise you picked, good luck! –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: see as the ideal grandparent? • Is my relationship with my adult child and partner strong and based on mutual respect? • Do I share parenting styles with my adult children? If not, can I support their style? When a new baby joins a family, everyone’s role changes, and every family member will experience this shift in their own way. Grandparents who experience this journey most successfully share some common traits. • They have a track record of positive, respectful interactions with their adult children (and their children’s partners). • They are able to put their adult children’s perspective on parenting above their own, by supporting their children’s goals for the grandchildren. • They accept that family life today will not be identical to the way life was when they had small children. Being a grandparent may be the most joyous for those who accept that they had their opportunity to raise their own family, and now, for their adult children, it’s their turn. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and now works exclusively with grandparents and their families. Cynthia and her husband, Gary, have lived in Piedmont for over 36 years and have raised two sons here. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents.
articles.title: A Grandparent is born

articles.text: Congratulations, you’re a grandparent! Is there any other significant life event over which we have so little control? We can’t determine the day of our birth and probably won’t orchestrate our death, but most folks put a lot of planning into every other step in their lives. Choice of career, choice of life partner, what city to live in, whether and when to have children, when to retire. But will you be a grandparent one day? Maybe…and maybe not. Some folks spend a decade or more anxiously waiting to hear that their adult child is starting a family, while others find the title of grandparent bestowed upon them when they least expect it. Some will end up with many grandchildren and struggle to get to know each one intimately, while others have one or two, and have a solid, regular role in their lives. Still other parents find that they never become grandparents, which is just fine for some, while many find it heartbreaking. What kind of grandparent will you be? Your concept is likely to be influenced by memories of your own grandparents, as well as the common depictions of grandparents that exist all around us. Many other factors shape our idea of what kind of grandparent we will be. We can’t determine the day of our birth and probably won’t orchestrate our death, but most folks put a lot of planning into every other step in their lives. Some folks spend a decade or more anxiously waiting to hear that their adult child is starting a family, while others find the title of grandparent bestowed upon them when they least expect it. Some will end up with many grandchildren and struggle to get to know each one intimately, while others have one or two, and have a solid, regular role in their lives. Still other parents find that they never become grandparents, which is just fine for some, while many find it heartbreaking. What kind of grandparent will you be? Your concept is likely to be influenced by memories of your own grandparents, as well as the common depictions of grandparents that exist all around us. Many other factors shape our idea of what kind of grandparent we will be. Here are some things to ask yourself: • Did I grow up with grandparents who played a strong role in my life? • Do I have a preconceived notion about what being a grandparent will be like? • Do I have a picture of what I see as the ideal grandparent? • Is my relationship with my adult child and partner strong and based on mutual respect? • Do I share parenting styles with my adult children? If not, can I support their style? When a new baby joins a family, everyone’s role changes, and every family member will experience this shift in their own way. Grandparents who experience this journey most successfully share some common traits. • They have a track record of positive, respectful interactions with their adult children (and their children’s partners). • They are able to put their adult children’s perspective on parenting above their own, by supporting their children’s goals for the grandchildren. • They accept that family life today will not be identical to the way life was when they had small children. Being a grandparent may be the most joyous for those who accept that they had their opportunity to raise their own family, and now, for their adult children, it’s their turn. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and now works exclusively with grandparents and their families. Cynthia and her husband, Gary, have lived in Piedmont for over 36 years and have raised two sons here. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Jill Biden with the presidential dogs, Major and Champ. By Abby, a Bernese Mountain Dog Dear Abby: Can you tell us anything about the First Dogs that now reside in the White House? I’m curious! –Tina and Dill the Frenchie Dear Tina and Dill: There are two male German Shepherds, named Major and Champ, now living in the White House. Major is about two years old, and is the first rescue dog to live in the White House. He loves running on the South Lawn while the 12-year-old Champ enjoys sleeping in the new dog bed by the fireplace. There are rumors that Major may help raise awareness and money for shelters. According to the First Lady, Jill Biden, a cat will soon be joining them. The last cat to live in the White House was Willie, a member of the George W. Bush family, and before that was Socks, the famous cat of Pres. Clinton. The White House was not completely finished when the first “First Dogs” moved in and began patrolling in the 1800’s. Bow wow, meow, –Abby Dear Abby: Is there any way dogs can help in the Pandemic? What can we do? –Ben and Olivia the Springer Spaniel Dear Ben and Olivia: I think the best you can do is to help each other to stay sane and safe until you get a vaccine. Apparently cuddling with a pet can lower blood pressure and diminish stress. Taking a walk or a hike (with a mask) is always helpful for general good health, so make a point to sneak out between rain showers and breathe. A dog in Turkey named Boncuk (beads) made a point of visiting the hospital her owner was taken to. Apparently, she would just wait by the hospital door from 9 a.m. until nightfall before returning home for dinner. A few times the owner’s family tried to bring her home early, but she would just return to the doors of the hospital. True loyalty. When the owner was finally released, Boncuk was wagging her tail and happily walking by the wheelchair as the owner hugged her. That’s a loyal dog. Tail wags to Boncuk, –Abby Dear Abby: I’d like to get my mom and dad a present for Valentine’s Day. Any ideas of what I can give them without going to a store? I’m not a good shopper but I’d like to say thanks. –Goose the rescued Mix Dear Goose: Bay Area artist Judy North can paint your mug for your folks so they will always have you on canvas and in their hearts. She’ll start by spending some time with you and snapping two to three rolls of film before painting you. Judy is a dog lover, and her goal is to capture your true spirit. Her work was shown on the walls of the Slanted Door restaurant in San Francisco for years. Check out her website at Judynorth.com. Or ask a family member to capture you in a drawing and then immortalize it on a cotton tote. Your folks will not only have a doggone image of you, but a piece of the family’s artwork, too. Cotton Tote Bag by Cece DuPraz comes with instructions, special paper, colored pencils and a ruler. The drawing you pick is then sent off and embroidered on the tote to have for a long, long time. Go to Neimanmarcus.com for more information. Lastly, there’s a magical book called The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse by Charlie Mackesy that not only inspires one to love animals but each other, no matter what shape or size or smell. Can’t wait to hear about which K9 surprise you picked, good luck! –Abby E-mail your comments, ideas and dog thoughts on any pet topic to Melanie Johnston at MSJ312@ aol.com.

articles.text: Joan (Jody) Earle, a beloved mother, grandmother, sister, and aunt, passed away on January 7, 2021 in Oakland, California. She was 89. Born Joan Christine Zuber on December 29, 1931 in Washington, DC, she was the daughter of Adolph and Alice Rita Zuber. She was known to all by her nickname Jody, which started when she was the editor of her high school newspaper and wrote a weekly column titled “Jody’s Jottings”. Her father was a Lt. Colonel in the Marine Corps, and she lived in many locations, including Pearl Harbor, Hawaii in 1941. She graduated from Hoover High School in San Diego California in 1949 and earned a bachelor’s degree in History in 1953 from the University of California in Berkeley. She also received a master’s degree in History at UC Berkeley in 1955. While in college she was a member of the Phi Mu sorority and the Prytanean Honor Society, which sought to promote the high ideas of scholarship, leadership, and service to the university and community. She went on to get teaching credentials in Elementary, Secondary, Community College and Special Education. She spent most of her adult life teaching children, including working with children with learning disabilities and tutoring. She was a substitute teacher in Piedmont and especially enjoyed teaching children who were classmates of her own six children. From 1989 to 2012 she taught multiple subjects at Fred French Youth Center in Oakland, a facility providing support for youth healing from trauma. She was well respected by family, friends, and students for her loving dedication to the learning and wellbeing of her students. Known for her kind gentle spirit, great sense of humor and smile she enchanted those who heard her retelling of the story of her family living in Pearl Harbor when it was attacked on Dec. 7, 1941. Quarters T, the house her family lived in on Ford Island, now with a plaque that reads “Zuber House” named after her family. Jody loved to read and write, leading her to write the book, The Children of Battleship Row, which gives generations of readers a glimpse of a 9-year old’s perspective of the attack on Pearl Harbor. She visited her home on Ford Island with her family many times making strong loving friendships with those she met. She loved and was loved by friends in the community, including Piedmont Community Church. She lived at Grand Lake Gardens in Oakland for the past eight years, She is survived by three sons, John Earle III (Jenny), David Earle (Jennifer), and Robert Earle, and three daughters, Alicia Utley (Jony), Meg Dengler (Mike), and Alison Earle. Jody is also survived by five grandchildren, Kristina and Kayla Utley, Katie Nolasco, Benjamin and Sarah Dengler. She is additionally survived by a sister, Margaret (Peggy) Unger, and three nephews a niece and numerous great nephews and nieces. Jody requested that a Celebration of Life be held and that she be cremated, and her ashes laid to rest in Hawaii. Because of the closures of restaurants and facilities at this time, this Celebration of Life will be held at a later date and an announcement will be made. articles.text: Jeanie Christopoulos, a longtime Piedmont resident and member of the Ascension Greek Orthodox Cathedral of Oakland, died peacefully in her sleep on December 19, 2020. She was 89. Born Jeanie Batestas on March 13, 1931 in Ogden, Utah, she was the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Gus Batestas. Jeanie was a bright child, successful in school and driven to achieve. At an early age she enjoyed studying the piano and voice. She relocated to California in the 1950’s where she would become exceptionally active in cultural, community and political affairs in the San Francisco Bay Area. In 1961, she married Bay Area real estate developer Dan Christopoulos in one of the first wedding ceremonies performed in the newly built Greek Orthodox Church of the Ascension, now the Cathedral of the Ascension. Jeanie and Dan, along with Rev. Tom Paris and other Ascension members served on the Building and Design Committee for the Community Center built adjacent to the Cathedral in the late 1970’s. It continues to be an integral part of the community today, hosting weddings, high school proms, as well as traditional Greek Orthodox celebrations throughout the year. Jeanie was generous and giving with her time, and an excellent, self-taught cook. She was honored to teach The Art of Baklava at Ascension’s annual Oakland Greek Festival and loved promoting the Festival by teaching baklava-making on a TV news show. Jeanie was an active volunteer in her community, beginning in her children’s schools. In 1970, she campaigned for Dr. Marcus Foster to be appointed as Superintendent of Schools for the Oakland Unified School District. In 1977, Jeanie joined The Cancer League, a nonprofit that funds groundbreaking, early-stage cancer research. Jeanie was extremely proud to have been the only two-term President from 1991 to 1993. The Oakland Museum Women’s Board White Elephant Sale would eventually become Jeantrips to Manhattan visits to galleries, dealers, and museums, where she fed her keen interest in Japanese Imari. Jeanie and Dan traveled the world together, adventuring to China and Africa. Especially dear to her were their annual summer and winter trips to Lake Tahoe for skiing, boating and quality time with family and friends. At home, Jeanie and Dan loved entertaining; their home was regularly buzzing with their nearest and dearest, sharing big dinners, and spirited socializing. She was a wily Bridge partner enjoying the friendship of the same group for decades. Jeanie loved the company of the Sewing Club, where most of the time more tales were spun than anything involving needle and thread. Jeanie was a devoted follower of professional sports, ready to go toe-to-toe with the men on any topic, especially the Warriors and her favorite player, Steph Curry. Never one to fall behind on current events, nothing gave Jeanie more joy than to sit and read the NY Times cover to cover, except maybe clipping articles of interest for her family. Jeanie is survived by her son Basil and his wife Shirley of Oakland; daughter Eleni Gianopulos and husband Randall of New York, and grandchildren Rebecca, Peter, William, and Sophia. She is also survived by sister-in-law Elaine Platias and brother-in-law Tasso Voulgares, and her godchildren, Pam and Dave Fullerton, and their children John, Anastasia and George. She is predeceased by her mother Elaine Batestas, and two sisters, Maria Batestas and Becky Voulgares. Due to Covid restrictions, private Trisagion and Funeral Services were held, with Interment following services at Mt. View Cemetery in Oakland. A celebration of Jeanie’s life will be held as soon as Covid restrictions allow. In lieu of flowers, the family asks that contributions in Jeanie’s memory be made to the Ascension Greek Orthodox Cathedral of Oakland, The Oakland Museum of California, or The Cancer League, Inc. articles.text: Being told I would be expected to talk here, I inquired what sort of talk I ought to make. They said it should be something suitable to youth – something didactic, instructive, or something in the nature of good advice. Very well. I have a few things in my mind which I have often longed to say for the instruction of the young; for it is in one’s tender early years that such things will best take root and be most enduring and most valuable. incomplete training. Some authorities hold that the young out not to lie at all. That of course is putting it rather stronger than necessary. While I cannot go quite so far as that, I do maintain, and I believe I am right, that the young ought to be temperate in the use of this great art until practice and experience shall give them that confidence, elegance, and precision which alone can make the accomplishment graceful and profitable. 1 First, then, I will say to you, my young friends – and I say it beseechingly, urgently – always obey your parents when they are present. This is the best policy in the long run, because if you don’t, they will make you. Most parents think they know better than you do, and you can generally make more by humoring that superstition than you can by acting on your own better judgment. 2 Be respectful to your superiors if you have any; also, to strangers, and sometimes to others. If a person offends you and you are in doubt as to whether it was intentional or not, do not resort to extreme measures. Simply watch your chance and hit him with a brick. That will be sufficient. If you shall find that he had not intended any offense, come out frankly and confess yourself in the wrong when you struck him. Acknowledge it like a man and say you didn’t mean to. Yes, always avoid violence; in this age of charity and kindliness, the time has gone by for such things. Leave dynamite to the low and unrefined. 3 Go to bed early, get up early – this is wise. Some authorities say get up with the sun; some say get up with one thing, others with another. But a lark is really the best thing to get up with. It gives you a splendid reputation with everybody to know that you get up with the lark; and if you get the right kind of lark, and work at him right, you can easily train him to get up at half past nine, every time – it’s no trick at all. 4 Now, as to the matter of lying, you want to be very careful about lying, otherwise you are nearly sure to get caught. Once caught, you can never again be in the eyes to the good and the pure what you were before. Many a young person has injured himself permanently through a single clumsy and ill-finished lie, the result of carelessness born of days ago, right in the next farm house to the one where I am spending the summer, a grandmother, old and gray and sweet, one of the loveliest spirits in the land, was sitting at her work, when her young grandson crept in and got down an old, battered, rusty gun which had not been touched for many years and was supposed not to be loaded, and pointed it at her, laughing and threatening to shoot. In her fright she ran screaming and pleading toward the door on the other side of the room; but as she passed him he placed the gun almost against her very breast and pulled the trigger! He had supposed it was not loaded. And he was right – it wasn’t. So, there wasn’t any harm done. It is the only case of that kind I ever heard of. Therefore, just the same, don’t you meddle with old, unloaded firearms; they are the most deadly and unerring things that have ever been created by man. You don’t have to take any pains at all with them; you don’t have to have a rest, you don’t have to have any sights on the gun, you don’t have to take aim, even. No, you just pick out a relative and bang away, and you are sure to get him. A youth who can’t hit a cathedral at thirty yards with a Gatling gun in three quarters of an hour, can take up an old empty musket and bag his grandmother every time, at a hundred. Think what Waterloo would have been if one of the armies had been boys armed with old muskets supposed not to be loaded, and the other army had been composed of their female relations. The very thought of it make one shudder. 6 There are many sorts of books; but good ones are the sort for the young to read – remember that. They are a great, an inestimable, and unspeakable means of improvement. Therefore, be careful in your selection, my young friends; be very careful; confine yourselves exclusively to Robertson’s Sermons, Baxter’s Saints’ Rest, The Innocents Abroad, and works of that kind. But I have said enough. I hope you will treasure up the instructions which I have given you, and make them a guide to your feet and a light to your understanding. articles.text: “The Grubb Company has been invited to continue its affiliation with Leading Real Estate Companies of the World and its luxury marketing division, Luxury Portfolio International,” owner DJ Grubb announced last week. Leading Real Estate Companies of the World is a global real estate community comprised of 550 real estate companies awarded membership based on rigorous standards for service and performance. With 4,600 offices and 135,000 sales associates in 70 countries, these firms represent 1.1 million global transactions annually. This affiliation empowers The Grubb Co. to combine its authentic local market leadership with top-ranked resources and relationships with other premier real estate firms across the country and around the world. The company participates in LeadingRE’s industry-leading referral network, which generates more than 30,000 referrals each year and allows The Grubb Co. to assist home buyers and sellers in virtually any market worldwide. In addition, the company has access to award-winning online and in-person learning programs and events, professional marketing resources, exclusive networking opportunities, and more. The Grubb Co. also benefits from its membership in Luxury Portfolio International (LPI), an exclusive group of LeadingRE companies that hold significant market share in the high-end. LPI attracts a global audience of visitors from over 200 countries/ territories every month and markets approximately 50,000 luxury homes annually. LPI gives The Grubb Co. powerful high-end listing presentation and marketing tools and unique opportunities to target high-net-worth buyers. “This association truly serves our clientele. We have been selected for membership because we represent the higher end of the market in our community. This association gives our properties worldwide qualified exposure. No other company in our marketplace has this unique Global footprint,” said Grubb. “We are delighted to have The Grubb Co. as part of our distinguished network of premier brokerages. The company has an impeccable reputation in the East Bay and is a valued part of our global community,” said Paul Boomsma, president and CEO of LeadingRE. “As a member of LeadingRE and LPI, the Grubb Co. combines authentic, local expertise with unparalleled global resources.” To learn more about Leading Real Estate Companies of the World®, visit www.LeadingRE. com. articles.text: This letter was sent to Piedmont City Council. Editor: I heard from a neighbor about the potential 7-year lease of a city-owned building to the Piedmont Center for the Arts. From what I understand, I am opposed. For what appears to be an unusually favorable deal that is wholly inconsistent with the treatment of other organizations right here in Piedmont, there would need to be a phenomenally compelling case to enter into this lease ... but I have not heard anything like that. When I was treasurer for a boy scout troop here, I wrote checks to the city of Piedmont for the use of city facilities. I know that other organizations do the same. As a board member for a nonprofit organization serving kids in the Oakland schools, I have never seen something like this and would find it unusual. In the name of consistency, transparency, and fiduciary responsibility, I ask you to find another approach. –Jonathan Becker
articles.title: Opposed to lease terms for PCA

articles.text: Editor: In the Post’s Letters to the Editor, Bernard Pech effectively outlined why Reach Codes should not encourage electric ranges. But there is so much more to back up his findings. He states, “an electric range, whether heating through resistive elements or by induction, generates three times more greenhouse gases than a natural gas range if the electricity feeding the home is produced by a natural gas power plant.” “The CA energy mix in 2019 was 43% natural gas, 8% nuclear and 17% hydroelectric. These plants, due to Carnot, resistive and electrostatic transmission loss and other factors, have an energy efficiency in converting gas to electricity of about 33% (PUC report 2017), and 79-95% of plants run at 29% efficiency. Therefore, an electric range can use as much as three (3) times more gas in cooking a meal than a natural gas range.” As a 40-year resident of Piedmont owning a 1915 home, I cannot afford to ADA upgrade my kitchen and bath if I have to convert to electricity. Just because Piedmont is a Charter City and is allowed to go beyond what is required by the State, does not mean that it is rational. You are restricting the upgrading (ADA or otherwise) of Piedmont older homes, especially those of older residents on fixed incomes and the disabled. –Pat Markovich Due to volume, there was not space for all letters. More letters will be printed next week. Cost of America’s Cheap Goods Books “A crude, hand-written note slipped into Halloween merchandise made in China leads Pang on a search for its author and introduces her to the nightmare life of Chinese prison labor, so-called re-education camps, the worst horrors of living in a police state, and lives destroyed just for being an independent thinker.” —Susan Thurin, Bookends On Main, Menomonie, WI

articles.text: A PHS Parent Club Meeting will be held on Thursday, February 4, at 7:00 p.m. PHS Principal Adam Littlefield, the PHS administration team and School Board President Cory Smegal will answer questions on PHS reopening. The schedules for in-person learning at Piedmont middle and high schools can only occur if Alameda County returns to the red tier of COVID restrictions by going under 7.0 new daily cases per 100,000 population for five days. Cases have been decreasing, as of Tuesday February 2 the adjusted new county daily case rate sat at 23.1 per 100,000 population. Piedmont High The proposed PHS schedule for in-person learning utilizes a schedule of only 9th and 10th graders on campus one week and only 11th and 12th grades on campus the next week. One half of students would attend class in the morning, and a new group would arrive in the afternoon. No one would be allowed on campus during lunchtime. This plan allows for smaller class sizes of 15 students. Principal Adam Littlefield’s video with details and explanation on the schedule can be viewed at: https://drive.google. com/file/d/12CWTPFRUcj8SKd- 6PVBKOlMvpQ3iDqmLN/view. Millennium High The Millennium High survey gives parents three options of learning models. Students can remain in distance learning, return just to classes at Millennium, or return to classes in-person at MHS and with PHS students. MHS can invite students onto campus for instruction more frequently than at PHS because all Millennium classes have 15 or fewer students. In week 1 of the proposed schedule Grades 9 and 10 would be invited for a full Tuesday to Friday week of in-person MHS classes. In week 2, Grades 11 and 12 would be invited for a full Tuesday-Friday week of in-person MHS classes. Principal Shannon Fierro’s five-minute video can be seen at: www.youtube.com/ watch?v=GrONsCoPm0g&feature=youtu.be. A key component to this plan is that even if COVID cases increase, schools in progress are allowed to stay open, as confirmed by Alameda County Public Health Director Dr. Nicholas Moss. As long as Kindergarten starts on February 9, the rest of the phased reopening can continue. “I am feeling more hopeful right now than I have felt in a long time,” said School Board president Cory Smegal at the board’s meeting on January 27. “Cases are decreasing, and Dr. Moss thinks the Red Tier may be possible in the next few weeks.” School Schedules Continued from page 1 A PHS Parent Club Meeting will be held on Thursday, February 4, at 7:00 p.m. PHS Principal Adam Littlefield, the PHS administration team and School Board President Cory Smegal will answer questions on PHS reopening. The schedules for in-person learning at Piedmont middle and high schools can only occur if Alameda County returns to the red tier of COVID restrictions by going under 7.0 new daily cases per 100,000 population for five days. Cases have been decreasing, as of Tuesday February 2 the adjusted new county daily case rate sat at 23.1 per 100,000 population. Piedmont High The proposed PHS schedule for in-person learning utilizes a schedule of only 9th and 10th graders on campus one week and only 11th and 12th grades on campus the next week. One half of students would attend class in the morning, and a new group would arrive in the afternoon. No one would be allowed on campus during lunchtime. This plan allows for smaller class sizes of 15 students. Principal Adam Littlefield’s video with details and explanation on the schedule can be viewed at: https://drive.google. com/file/d/12CWTPFRUcj8SKd- 6PVBKOlMvpQ3iDqmLN/view. Millennium High The Millennium High survey gives parents three options of learning models. Students can remain in distance learning, return just to classes at Millennium, or return to classes in-person at MHS and with PHS students. MHS can invite students onto campus for instruction more frequently than at PHS because all Millennium classes have 15 or fewer students. In week 1 of the proposed schedule Grades 9 and 10 would be invited for a full Tuesday to Friday week of in-person MHS classes. In week 2, Grades 11 and 12 would be invited for a full Tuesday-Friday week of in-person MHS classes. Principal Shannon Fierro’s five-minute video can be seen at: www.youtube.com/ watch?v=GrONsCoPm0g&feature=youtu.be. Piedmont Middle School Piedmont Middle School’s proposed in-person schedule uses a “Two Period Rotating Trimester Model.” Only one grade level at a time would be on campus during “2 period blocks.” This amounts to each student having half a day of in-person learning (two periods) once per week. The other five periods would continue with distance learning. Depending upon how much time is left in the school year when allowed to start, the schedule would be divided into three equal parts or trimesters. If there are 15 weeks left when class starts each trimester would be five weeks. For example, in the first trimester 6th graders would be on campus for periods 1 and 3 in the morning on Tuesdays or Thursday. Then in the 2nd trimester 6th grades would have periods 5 and 7 in the afternoons Tuesday or Thursday. Finally, in the last trimester they would have periods 4 and 6 in-person Wednesday or Friday. There would be two different groups of each grade, on campus different days. No 2nd period classes would be offered this year in this plan at the middle school. Principal Ryan Fletcher’s reopening plan video is available for viewing at: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1rPXug-t20_WASiogWUhipd0iLS1SdPKn/view. 6th graders may not have to wait so long however as they have been included in Newsom’s K-6 Safe Schools for All Plan and are slated to return on February 23. All grades from TK to 12th will have distance learning exclusively every Monday. articles.text: Piedmont Police interrupted an attempted auto theft on Hazel Lane at 4:03 a.m. on Friday January 29. Upon seeing the patrol car, a woman jumped into a nearby stolen car with a male accomplice. Hazel Lane is a full loop, so when the car came back, the officer was waiting for it. The male suspect got out of the car and started running away. The woman got into the driver’s seat and raced off in the car. Further down the street, the woman ditched the vehicle and ran away. The police requested backup assistance from Oakland PD, including a K9 unit. The female suspect was located and arrested. A search of the stolen vehicle produced stolen mail, a shaved key, suspected methamphetamine, and paraphernalia. It was determined that the woman was on probation and was transported to Santa Rita jail. The stolen vehicle was recovered and returned to the owner.

pages.text: 32 Wednesday, February 3, 2021 Reach Codes Continued from page 1 Some of the key components of the reach codes are shown below. More details can be found on the City’s website, or talk to a member of the Planning and Building Department when you apply for a permit. • Newly constructed low-rise residential buildings and new detached ADU’s must use all electric building appliances. No gas lines can be hooked up to these buildings. • Projects that include an entirely new level or expand the total roof area by 30% or more, must install solar panels on the roof. • A renovation project that costs $25,000 or more must include an energy efficient insulation or heating system electrification improvement to include in the renovation. • A renovation project that costs $100,000 or more must include two energy efficient insulation or heating system electrification improvements to include in the renovation. • • • • • The energy efficient insulation or heating system requirement can be modified with a Home Energy Score of at least a 7 completed in the last five years. This modification is included so homes that have been pursuing energy efficiency measures can be recognized for their efforts. An application for an electrical panel upgrade must include capacity in the panel to accommodate future electrification of all appliances in the residence. An application for a kitchen or laundry area renovation must include electrical outlets for future appliance installations. At point of listing for sale of a property, a report from a Home Energy Audit or Home Energy Score must be provided to potential buyers and submitted to the City. Notably, many of these requirements will not affect most projects in Piedmont. Approximately 20 to 25 percent of renovation projects cost over $25,000. As stated before, the reach codes were put in place in order to reduce Piedmont’s natural gas emissions. Over 90 percent of emissions come from Piedmont residential living units. The reach codes are intended to slow natural gas usage, while still meeting the community standards that were published in the City’s Climate Action Plan. Piedmont is not alone in this initiative. Dozens of municipalities have passed reach codes in California. The California Energy Commission’s next update of statewide building codes (Title 24) will be implemented in 2023. Until then, these reach codes will help Piedmont homes become more energy efficient while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. For questions, please contact the planner working on your home renovation, or the City’s Sustainability Program Manager, Alyssa Dykman. CRIME REPORT By Jay Russell Auto theft interrupted, vehicle ditched, 1 arrest Piedmont Police interrupted an attempted auto theft on Hazel Lane at 4:03 a.m. on Friday January 29. Upon seeing the patrol car, a woman jumped into a nearby stolen car with a male accomplice. Hazel Lane is a full loop, so when the car came back, the officer was waiting for it. The male suspect got out of the car and started running away. The woman got into the driver’s seat and raced off in the car. Further down the street, the woman ditched the vehicle and ran away. The police requested backup assistance from Oakland PD, including a K9 unit. The female suspect was located and arrested. A search of the stolen vehicle produced stolen mail, a shaved key, suspected methamphetamine, and paraphernalia. It was determined that the woman was on probation and was transported to Santa Rita jail. The stolen vehicle was recovered and returned to the owner. Where in the World Are We?
